title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
生而知之者上也
李登
同考試官敎諭殷批〔削蔓剔浮獨標理奥蓋傑作也〕
同考試官敎諭鍾批〔詞氣渾涵文之近古者〕
考試官敎授黄批〔光彩内蘊其色蒼然〕
考試官敎授郭批〔發生知及上字意明徹〕
===
聖人論知而以性諸天者爲至也蓋生而神明
則知以天矣非天下之至聖其孰能與於斯宜
夫子首列之以啓天下求知之學也今夫人受
衷於天地以生孰不有此理之當知與眞知之
在我者乎顧所稟不齊而知因以異是故有生
而知之者焉清明在躬之神潛會夫性眞而因
生以具者不隨生而漸移虚靈不昧之體夙契
夫道妙而以形而寓者不爲形之所囿其本然
者常瑩而未甞汩也故率其天德之良知一觸
punctuated:
第壹場

四書

「生而知之者，上也。」

李登

同考試官敎諭殷批：〔削蔓剔浮，獨標理奥，蓋傑作也。〕
同考試官敎諭鍾批：〔詞氣渾涵，文之近古者。〕
考試官敎授黄批：〔光彩内蘊，其色蒼然。〕
考試官敎授郭批：〔發「生知」及「上」字意，明徹。〕

聖人論知，而以性諸天者爲至也。蓋生而神明，則知以天矣。非天下之至聖，其孰能與於斯？宜夫子首列之，以啓天下求知之學也。今夫人受衷於天地以生，孰不有此理之當知，與眞知之在我者乎？顧所稟不齊，而知因以異，是故有生而知之者焉。清明在躬之神，潛會夫性眞，而因生以具者，不隨生而漸移；虚靈不昧之體，夙契夫道妙，而以形而寓者，不爲形之所囿。其本然者常瑩而未甞汩也，故率其天德之良知，一觸
translation_en:
First Session

The Four Books

"Those who are born with knowledge are the highest."

Li Deng 李登

Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Yin 殷 comments: 〔Pruning away overgrown vines and stripping off superficialities, it uniquely highlights the profound depths of principle; it is indeed a masterpiece.〕
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Zhong 鍾 comments: 〔Its diction and vital breath are deep and all-embracing—a piece of writing approaching antiquity.〕
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Huang 黄 comments: 〔Its brilliance is contained within, its hue venerable and antique.〕
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Guo 郭 comments: 〔It elucidates the meaning of "born with knowledge" and the word "highest" with clarity and penetration.〕

When the Sage discusses knowledge, he regards that which is endowed as nature from Heaven as the ultimate. Indeed, when one is born with spiritual intelligence, one's knowledge comes by way of Heaven. Were one not the most sagely person in the world, who could partake in this? Rightly did the Master place this first in order to inspire the pursuit of learning and knowledge throughout the world. Now, among human beings who receive their moral nature from Heaven and Earth at birth, who does not possess this principle that ought to be known and the true knowledge that resides within oneself? Yet because their endowments are not uniform, their knowing consequently differs; for this reason, there are those who are born with knowledge. The spirit of pure clarity residing in their person silently communes with the truth of human nature, and that which is complete by virtue of birth does not gradually shift along with life's course; the unclouded, numinous, and vacío substance early on tallies with the subtlety of the Way, and that which lodges within physical form is not confined by form. What is original in them is ever lustrous and has never been muddied; therefore, following the innate knowledge of their heavenly virtue, at a single touch…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
而上下俱融不必啟知於見聞而凡窮理以爲
知者不能外矣其炯然者常覺而未甞泯也故
任其自然之明覺一悟而表裏俱洞不必知新
於耳目而凡格物以致知者不是過矣之人也
完太極二五之眞而寵綏於維皇者獨隆應貞
元會合之運而間值於天地者不偶氣之清通
極於命其生篤生也是殆聰明睿智之至聖固
將縱之以首出之資者也質之粹不離於天其
知天知也是殆先知先覺之天民固特授之以
===
獨稟之智者也故就其等斯謂之上而求之天
下何可以易見哉要之知者在天者也學者在
人者也天下不皆生知也而盡人以成天及其
知之一矣故學則次於上而不學斯爲下玆學
之不可已而夫子勉人之至意其在斯與然則
生知者可遂廢學哉夫孔子聖矣而好古敏求
且日孳孳焉堯之欽明舜之濬哲非上乎而猶
兢兢業業以從事于學聖人之不純任乎天也
如此有生知之質者而又學焉堯舜學爲孔子
punctuated: 而上下俱融，不必啟知於見聞，而凡窮理以爲知者，不能外矣；其炯然者常覺而未甞泯也，故任其自然之明覺，一悟而表裏俱洞，不必知新於耳目，而凡格物以致知者，不是過矣。之人也，完太極二五之眞，而寵綏於維皇者獨隆；應貞元會合之運，而間值於天地者不偶。氣之清通極於命，其生，篤生也，是殆聰明睿智之至聖，固將縱之以首出之資者也；質之粹不離於天，其知，天知也，是殆先知先覺之天民，固特授之以獨稟之智者也。故就其等斯謂之上，而求之天下，何可以易見哉！要之，知者在天者也，學者在人者也。天下不皆生知也，而盡人以成天，及其知之，一矣。故學則次於上，而不學斯爲下，玆學之不可已，而夫子勉人之至意，其在斯與！然則生知者可遂廢學哉？夫孔子聖矣，而好古敏求，且日孳孳焉；堯之欽明、舜之濬哲，非上乎？而猶兢兢業業以從事于學。聖人之不純任乎天也如此。有生知之質者，而又學焉堯、舜，學爲孔子，
translation_en: …and both the higher and lower principles are thoroughly harmonized. One need not awaken knowledge through seeing and hearing, yet none who exhaust principle to attain knowledge can go beyond this. That which is radiantly bright in him is ever-awakened and has never been extinguished; therefore, relying on his natural luminous awareness, at a single realization both the inner and outer are completely penetrated. One need not acquire new knowledge through the ears and eyes, yet none who investigate things to extend knowledge can surpass this. Such a person preserves intact the true essence of the Supreme Ultimate, yin and yang, and the Five Phases, and the favor and tranquility bestowed upon him by the August Heaven are uniquely abundant; he responds to the cosmic cycle where firmness and origination converge, and his rare appearance between heaven and earth is no mere coincidence. The clarity and penetration of his vital energy reach the utmost limit of destiny—his birth is a specially favored birth. He is indeed a supreme sage of quickness of apprehension,明 clarity of vision, far-reaching intelligence, and all-embracing wisdom, whom Heaven has surely endowed with the natural capacity to rise above the multitude. The purity of his substance never departs from Heaven—his knowledge is Heavenly knowledge. He is indeed one of Heaven's people who is first to know and first to awaken, upon whom has surely been specially conferred a uniquely endowed wisdom. Therefore, in terms of his rank, this is called the highest; yet if one seeks such a person in the world, how could he be easily found? In sum, innate knowledge pertains to Heaven, whereas learning pertains to man. Not everyone in the world is born with knowledge, yet when one exhausts human effort to fulfill the Heavenly endowment, by the time one comes to know it, it is one and the same. Therefore, those who learn rank next to the highest, while those who do not learn are the lowest. Thus learning must never cease—and does not the Master's utmost intention in encouraging people lie right here? Even so, can those who are born with knowledge simply abandon learning? Now, Confucius was a sage, yet he loved the ancients and was earnest in seeking knowledge, working tirelessly day by day. Were not Yao, with his reverent intelligence, and Shun, with his profound wisdom, of the highest rank? Yet they still devoted themselves to learning with cautious diligence. Such is the way the sages did not rely purely upon Heaven! If one who possesses the nature of being born with knowledge also learns from [?] Yao and Shun, and learns to be like Confucius,…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
則知益神矣
待其人而後行故曰苟不至德至道不凝
焉
曾鳳儀
同考試官教諭朱批有體認能發揮
同考試官學正蕭批直紓真見意旨翛然千言一澤也
道德者乎高薦允宜
考試官教授黄批思致精密詞意温粹
考試官教授郭批冲淡中有奇氣
===
中庸以行道屬諸人而必申言其不虛行也蓋
德者疑道之本也苟無其德其何以行之哉中
庸明人道也意若曰大哉聖人之道無外無内
斯其至矣然豈無所待而行哉涵於太虛其體
不能有為也而以人為體恒待人以成其能原
於天命其用不能自顯也而以人為用恒待人
而運其化合之而天地萬物孰統體是必有致
中和者出焉而後位育之效行于兩間也析之
而禮儀威儀孰推行是必有觀會通者出焉而
punctuated:
則知益神矣。

「待其人而後行。故曰：苟不至德，至道不凝焉。」
曾鳳儀
同考試官教諭朱批：有體認，能發揮。
同考試官學正蕭批：直紓真見，意旨翛然，千言一澤也，道德者乎？高薦允宜。
考試官教授黄批：思致精密，詞意温粹。
考試官教授郭批：冲淡中有奇氣。

《中庸》以行道屬諸人，而必申言其不虛行也。蓋德者，疑道之本也；苟無其德，其何以行之哉？《中庸》明人道也，意若曰：大哉聖人之道，無外無内，斯其至矣，然豈無所待而行哉？涵於太虛，其體不能有為也，而以人為體，恒待人以成其能；原於天命，其用不能自顯也，而以人為用，恒待人而運其化。合之而天地萬物，孰統體是？必有致中和者出焉，而後位育之效行于兩間也。析之而禮儀威儀，孰推行是？必有觀會通者出焉，而
translation_en:
… then one's knowledge becomes all the more marvelous.

"It awaits the proper person before it can be put into practice. Hence it is said: 'Unless there is supreme virtue, the supreme Way cannot be consolidated.'"
Zeng Fengyi 曾鳳儀
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Zhu 朱: Shows personal realization and is able to elaborate the theme.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Instructor Xiao 蕭: Directly sets forth genuine insight; its purport is unconstrained and clear. Is he not one steeped in the Way and its virtue [?] (千言一澤也道德者乎)? High recommendation is truly fitting.
Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Instructor Huang 黄: The train of thought is precise and dense; the diction and meaning are gentle and pure.
Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Instructor Guo 郭: Amidst calm simplicity there is an extraordinary vigor.

The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong 中庸) assigns the practicing of the Way to human beings, and necessarily reiterates that it is not practiced in vain. For virtue is the foundation for consolidating [reading 凝 for 疑] the Way; if one lacks that virtue, how can one put it into practice? In clarifying the Way of humanity, the Doctrine of the Mean intends to say: Great indeed is the Way of the Sage! With nothing outside it and nothing inside it, it is truly supreme; yet how could it be put into practice without awaiting anything? Contained within the Great Vacuity, its substance cannot act on its own, so it takes human beings as its substance and constantly awaits human beings to bring its capacities to completion. Originating in the Mandate of Heaven, its function cannot manifest itself on its own, so it takes human beings as its function and constantly awaits human beings to set its transformations in motion. Taken together as a whole, as for Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things, who integrates and embodies them? Only when someone who achieves equilibrium and harmony emerges are the effects of establishing Heaven and Earth in their proper places and nourishing the myriad things carried out between Heaven and Earth. Analyzed in detail, as for the three hundred rules of ceremony and three thousand rules of demeanor, who puts them into practice? Only when someone who perceives their convergence and continuity emerges…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
後經緯之章敷于羣動也是行道之必待於人
如此而道其可以虛行哉故曰苟不至德至道
不凝焉蓋道與德一也得此之謂德固道之所
待以行者也苟非其人則中之所存未能完性
命之眞而知之所格不能達神明之蘊雖洋洋
者固流動而未嘗息也而無德以統體之則其
極于天而殽于物者亦象焉而已矣而與吾心
固自爲二也其何能凝斯道之全體而賛其化
育哉雖優優者固充足而未嘗間也而無德以
===
推行之則其經而等曲而殺者亦迹焉而已矣
而與吾身固自有間也其何以會斯道之妙用
而行其典禮哉信乎道不能自行而亦不可以
虛行也脩德凝道之功其可緩乎抑論道體本
虛而體道貴實三千三百固天地萬物之實理
也此下學存心致知之功自可以定命而上達
天德故論行道而曰凝道其實意可想已推其
極則經緯文章先王之所以官天地宰萬物用
是道也彼世之蔑禮教隳聞見者吾不知其視
punctuated: 後經緯之章敷于羣動也。是行道之必待於人如此，而道其可以虛行哉？故曰：「苟不至德，至道不凝焉。」蓋道與德一也，得此之謂德，固道之所待以行者也。苟非其人，則中之所存未能完性命之眞，而知之所格不能達神明之蘊。雖洋洋者固流動而未嘗息也，而無德以統體之，則其極于天而殽于物者，亦象焉而已矣，而與吾心固自爲二也。其何能凝斯道之全體，而賛其化育哉？雖優優者固充足而未嘗間也，而無德以推行之，則其經而等、曲而殺者，亦迹焉而已矣，而與吾身固自有間也。其何以會斯道之妙用，而行其典禮哉？信乎道不能自行，而亦不可以虛行也，脩德凝道之功，其可緩乎？抑論道體本虛，而體道貴實。三千三百，固天地萬物之實理也。此下學存心致知之功，自可以定命而上達天德。故論行道而曰「凝道」，其實意可想已。推其極，則經緯文章，先王之所以官天地、宰萬物，用是道也。彼世之蔑禮教、隳聞見者，吾不知其視…
translation_en:
…only then are the patterns of its warp and woof spread throughout the myriad movements of the world. Since the practice of the Way depends upon human beings to such a degree, how could the Way be practiced in the abstract? Thus it is said: "If there be not perfect virtue, the perfect Way cannot be consolidated."

For the Way and virtue are one. To attain this Way in oneself is what is called virtue, which is indeed that upon which the Way depends in order to be practiced. If one is not such a person, then what is preserved within cannot bring to completion the truth of human nature and heaven's decree, and what is investigated by knowledge cannot penetrate the depths of spiritual intelligence. Although that which is vast and overflowing [the Way in its macrocosmic aspect] certainly flows on without ever ceasing, if there is no virtue to embody it as a whole, then its reaching up to heaven and its interweaving through all things remain mere phenomena, altogether separate from one's own mind. How then could one consolidate the complete substance of this Way and assist in its transforming and nourishing work? And although that which is abundant and ample [the Way in its ritual aspect] is certainly full and without any gap, if there is no virtue to carry it out, then its regular gradations and its detailed diminutions remain mere outward traces, altogether standing apart from one's own person. How then could one grasp the wondrous functioning of this Way and put its canons and rites into practice? Truly, the Way cannot practice itself, nor can it be practiced in vain! Can the effort of cultivating virtue to consolidate the Way be delayed?

Moreover, while the substance of the Way is originally vacuous, embodying the Way values substantiality. The three hundred major and three thousand minor rules of ritual are indeed the substantial principles of heaven, earth, and the myriad things. Below, this effort of learning—preserving the mind and extending knowledge—can naturally establish one's destiny and, above, reach heavenly virtue. Therefore, when discussing the practice of the Way, the text speaks of "consolidating the Way"; its practical intention can easily be imagined. Pushed to its ultimate, the warp and woof of cultural pattern—that whereby the former kings governed heaven and earth and ruled the myriad things—was through the use of this very Way. As for those in the world who slight ritual teaching and discard learning and observation, I do not know how they view…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
天地萬物又何如也行道者其辨之
天下大悅書曰丕顯哉文王謨丕承哉武
王烈佑啓我後人咸以正無缺
李際春
同考試官學正趙批此作窽深研精華實並茂周公
相業宛然見之
同考試官教授周批提掇照應處神彩動人
考試官教授黄批醇雅明暢
考試官教授郭批順暢可式
===
大賢賛元聖大順之治而必徵諸書焉蓋文武
之謨烈盛矣而實周公成之也此天下之所以
悅其治與昔孟子釋公都子好辨之疑及此若
曰世之治也有啓運之君則必有翼運之臣吾
甞觀于有周而知周公一代之治功矣蓋文武
嗣興雖足以對天下之心而害有未除民之望
治猶未已也周公相武王而悉殄其害焉夫是
以民安於撥亂而萬邦仰奠麗之休物阜於勝
殘而羣生蒙煦育之利有夏固已脩和矣玆則
punctuated:
天地萬物又何如也？行道者其辨之。

天下大悅。《書》曰：「丕顯哉，文王謨！丕承哉，武王烈！佑啓我後人，咸以正無缺。」
李際春
同考試官學正趙批：此作窽深研精，華實並茂，周公相業宛然見之。
同考試官教授周批：提掇照應處，神彩動人。
考試官教授黄批：醇雅明暢。
考試官教授郭批：順暢可式。

大賢賛元聖大順之治，而必徵諸《書》焉。蓋文、武之謨烈盛矣，而實周公成之也，此天下之所以悅其治與！昔孟子釋公都子好辨之疑及此，若曰：世之治也，有啓運之君，則必有翼運之臣。吾甞觀于有周，而知周公一代之治功矣。蓋文、武嗣興，雖足以對天下之心，而害有未除，民之望治猶未已也。周公相武王，而悉殄其害焉。夫是以民安於撥亂，而萬邦仰奠麗之休；物阜於勝殘，而羣生蒙煦育之利。有夏固已脩和矣，玆則
translation_en:
… Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things? Those who practice the Way ought to discern this.

"All under Heaven greatly rejoiced. The Book of Documents (Shu) says: 'How grandly illustrious were the plans of King Wen! How grandly carried forward were the achievements of King Wu! They aided and enlightened us, their descendants, so that all are correct and without defect.'"
Li Jichun 李際春
Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Instructor Zhao 趙 comments: This essay probes deeply and refines the essentials, flourishing in both flower and fruit; the ministerial achievements of the Duke of Zhou are vividly revealed in it.
Associate Examiner and Prefectural Instructor Zhou 周 comments: In the places where it lifts up the theme and creates structural correspondences, its spirited radiance moves the reader.
Examiner and Prefectural Instructor Huang 黄 comments: Pure, elegant, clear, and fluent.
Examiner and Prefectural Instructor Guo 郭 comments: Smooth and fluent, worthy of serving as a model.

The great worthy praises the supreme sage's governance of great harmony, and necessarily verifies it by reference to the Book of Documents. Indeed, the plans and achievements of King Wen and King Wu were flourishing, yet in truth it was the Duke of Zhou who brought them to completion. Is this not why all under Heaven rejoiced in his governance! Of old, when Mencius resolved Gongduzi's 公都子 doubt about his fondness for disputation and touched upon this, it was as if to say: When the world is well governed, if there is a ruler who inaugurates the dynastic fortune, there must also be a minister who assists that fortune. I have observed the house of Zhou and come to know the governing merit of the Duke of Zhou for an entire generation. Indeed, when King Wen and King Wu arose in succession, although they were sufficient to answer the hearts of all under Heaven, while harms remained unremoved, the people's longing for order still had not ceased. The Duke of Zhou assisted King Wu and completely eradicated those harms. Therefore, the people found peace in the suppression of rebellion, and the myriad states looked up to the blessings of settled attachment; things became abundant through the overcoming of cruelty, and all living beings received the benefit of warm nourishment. The realm of Xia had assuredly already been brought into cultivated harmony, and now…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
太和洋溢而民悅益爲之無疆四方固已攸同
矣玆則至治浹洽而民心益爲之胥慶此固周
公輔相之功有以光昭於前而垂裕於後者也
書不云乎丕顯哉文王謨丕承哉武王烈佑啓
我後人咸以正無缺蓋丕顯以開厥後文謨固
無斁也而實周公勤施于上下俾遹駿之聲愈
顯於無窮而謨之盡善者爲可傳焉丕承以貽
孫謀武烈固無競也而實周公翼賛於先後俾
纘緒之業愈承於不替而烈之盡美者爲可久
===
焉以覲文王之耿光子道盡而父道益著以揚
武王之大烈臣道盡而君道益隆此所以致天
下之悅而唐虞之盛復見于成周也然則頌文
武之德者詎可忘周公之功而一代之治允有
以纘禹之績歟雖然天下悅矣公之憂未釋也
無逸陳矣豳風誦矣桑土綢繆赤舄几几矣且
吐哺握髮繼日待旦憂愈深焉若其責之未塞
者凡以成終始之大忠而立萬世之臣極耳孟
子之所願學者夢周公之志也不得行其道而
punctuated: 太和洋溢，而民悅益爲之無疆；四方固已攸同矣，玆則至治浹洽，而民心益爲之胥慶。此固周公輔相之功，有以光昭於前而垂裕於後者也。《書》不云乎：「丕顯哉，文王謨！丕承哉，武王烈！佑啓我後人，咸以正無缺。」蓋丕顯以開厥後，文謨固無斁也，而實周公勤施于上下，俾遹駿之聲愈顯於無窮，而謨之盡善者爲可傳焉；丕承以貽孫謀，武烈固無競也，而實周公翼賛於先後，俾纘緒之業愈承於不替，而烈之盡美者爲可久焉。以覲文王之耿光，子道盡而父道益著；以揚武王之大烈，臣道盡而君道益隆。此所以致天下之悅，而唐虞之盛復見于成周也。然則頌文武之德者，詎可忘周公之功，而一代之治允有以纘禹之績歟？雖然，天下悅矣，公之憂未釋也。《無逸》陳矣，《豳風》誦矣，桑土綢繆，赤舄几几矣。且吐哺握髮，繼日待旦，憂愈深焉，若其責之未塞者，凡以成終始之大忠，而立萬世之臣極耳。孟子之所願學者，夢周公之志也；不得行其道，而
translation_en: …supreme harmony overflowed, and the people's delight grew ever more boundless because of it. The four quarters had indeed already been united; now supreme governance permeated everywhere, and the people's hearts rejoiced together all the more because of it. This was truly the achievement of the Duke of Zhou's assistance as minister, which cast glorious light upon his predecessors and bequeathed abundance to posterity. Does not the Book of Documents say: "Greatly illustrious were the plans of King Wen! Greatly continued were the achievements of King Wu! They aided and enlightened us, their descendants, all in rectitude and without defect." Indeed, in being greatly illustrious so as to open the way for his descendants, the plans of King Wen were certainly tireless; yet in reality it was the Duke of Zhou who diligently applied them above and below, causing his great reputation to shine ever more brightly into infinity, so that plans that were utterly good could be transmitted. In greatly continuing them so as to leave counsels for his grandsons, the achievements of King Wu were certainly peerless; yet in reality it was the Duke of Zhou who assisted before and after, causing the enterprise of continuing the patrimony to be carried on ever more unceasingly, so that achievements that were utterly noble could endure. By displaying the bright glory of King Wen, the way of the son was fulfilled and the way of the father became all the more manifest; by extolling the great achievements of King Wu, the way of the subject was fulfilled and the way of the ruler became all the more exalted. This was how he brought about the delight of all under Heaven, and how the flourishing of Tang and Yu was seen once again in Established Zhou. If that is so, how could those who praise the virtue of Kings Wen and Wu forget the merit of the Duke of Zhou, whereby the governance of an entire dynasty truly continued the accomplishments of Yu? Even so, when all under Heaven was delighted, the Duke's anxieties were still not relieved. "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi) was presented, the "Airs of Bin" (Binfeng) were recited, the mulberry-root soil was bound tightly around the nest, and his red slippers were calm and composed. Moreover, spitting out his food and grasping his hair to receive worthy men, continuing the day into night and waiting for the dawn, his anxieties grew ever deeper, as though his responsibilities had not yet been fulfilled—all simply to complete the great loyalty of beginning and end, and to establish the supreme standard for subjects for ten thousand generations. What Mencius wished to learn was the ambition that made Confucius dream of the Duke of Zhou; unable to put his Way into practice, and…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
來好辯之譏可以觀世矣
易
上九鼎玉鉉大吉无不利象曰玉鉉在上
剛柔節也
呂應和
同考試官教諭朱批發揮剛柔不偏意親切有味
同考試官學正蕭批得周孔本意結語尤有深思遠
識録之
考試官教授黄批理明詞達
===
考試官教授郭批體裁偉然
二聖交以相道美鼎爻爲其業隆而德純也甚
矣大業本於盛德也剛柔節而相德純矣聖人
之致美於象占也有以哉今夫天下重器也人
主舉而寄之相猶之舉鼎而寄之鉉也鼎之上
九以陽居陰有中德焉其象不唯鉉而鉉且玉
矣周公因其德之全而美其業也曰鼎玉鉉大
吉无不利則是一啓沃焉而如琢如磨之訓足
以導我宸聰而百倍仰圭璋之令望一舉措焉
punctuated:
來好辯之譏，可以觀世矣。

易

上九，鼎玉鉉，大吉，无不利。象曰：玉鉉在上，剛柔節也。

呂應和
同考試官教諭朱批：發揮剛柔不偏意，親切有味。
同考試官學正蕭批：得周孔本意，結語尤有深思遠識，録之。
考試官教授黄批：理明詞達。
考試官教授郭批：體裁偉然。

二聖交以相道美鼎爻，爲其業隆而德純也。甚矣，大業本於盛德也！剛柔節而相德純矣，聖人之致美於象占也有以哉！今夫天下，重器也；人主舉而寄之相，猶之舉鼎而寄之鉉也。鼎之上九，以陽居陰，有中德焉，其象不唯鉉，而鉉且玉矣。周公因其德之全而美其業也，曰「鼎玉鉉，大吉，无不利」。則是一啓沃焉，而如琢如磨之訓，足以導我宸聰，而百倍仰圭璋之令望；一舉措焉，
translation_en:
… incurred the criticism of being fond of disputing. From this one may observe the state of the world!

Book of Changes (Yi)

"Top Nine: The cauldron has rings of jade. Great good fortune; nothing that is not advantageous. The Commentary on the Images says: 'The rings of jade are at the very top: hardness and softness find their due measure.'"

Lü Yinghe 呂應和
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Zhu 朱: He elaborates the idea of hardness and softness being without bias in an intimate and flavorful manner.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Xiao 蕭: He grasps the original meaning of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, and his concluding words especially show deep thought and far-reaching insight. Record it for publication.
Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Huang 黃: The principles are clear and the phrasing is fluent.
Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Guo 郭: Its form and style are magnificent.

The two Sages both praise the line of the Cauldron hexagram in terms of the Way of the chief minister, because his enterprise is lofty and his virtue pure. How true it is that a great enterprise is rooted in abundant virtue! When hardness and softness find their due measure, the virtue of the chief minister is pure; there is indeed a reason why the Sages bestowed such praise in the image and the prognostication! Now the Empire is a weighty vessel. When the ruler takes it up and entrusts it to a chief minister, it is just like taking up a cauldron and entrusting it to its lifting rings. In the Top Nine of the Cauldron hexagram, a yang line occupies a yin position, possessing the virtue of centrality; its image is not merely that of lifting rings, but of rings that are moreover made of jade. Because of the completeness of his virtue, the Duke of Zhou praised his enterprise, saying, "The cauldron has rings of jade. Great good fortune; nothing that is not advantageous." Thus, whenever he offers counsel to enlighten the sovereign, his teachings—refined as if carved and polished—suffice to guide the imperial hearing, while the百官 [hundred officials] look up to his fine reputation, pure as a jade tablet; whenever he takes an action or puts a measure in place, …

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
而不競不絿之政足以式是下國而九服蒙潤
澤之宏庥鴻業固而鼎命之所以不替者此也
邦與家而永孚矣雉膏食而鼎實之所以不究
者此也名與位而俱盛矣謂之玉鉉而大吉且
利也豈惟无虞於覆餗而已哉眞足以配金鉉
之君而垂慶於有永矣乃夫子因其業之隆而
本其德曰剛柔節也則是高明而柔克克者乃
所以爲剛用而神氣之所舒發動若有限而不
踰沉潛而剛克克者又所以爲柔用而元氣之
===
所渾涵時或有振而不靡人見其張弛之交濟
而不知自其溫潤而栗者劑之也人見其泰和
而不偏而不知本其純粹以精者出之也謂之
曰剛柔節也豈惟无病於掩瑜而已哉眞足以
當玉鉉之實而流光於无窮矣然則爲人臣者
非相業之難而相德之難非相德之難而協於
中者難也二聖交美而交發其義有以哉抑兩
觀三都之政夾谷之役蓋有時見其剛柔而未
竟者夫子寧无感也周公至矣雖然以公玉鉉
punctuated: 而不競不絿之政，足以式是下國，而九服蒙潤澤之宏庥。鴻業固而鼎命之所以不替者，此也，邦與家而永孚矣；雉膏食而鼎實之所以不究者，此也，名與位而俱盛矣。謂之「玉鉉」而「大吉」且「利」也，豈惟无虞於覆餗而已哉？眞足以配金鉉之君，而垂慶於有永矣！乃夫子因其業之隆而本其德，曰「剛柔節也」。則是高明而柔克，克者乃所以爲剛用，而神氣之所舒發，動若有限而不踰；沉潛而剛克，克者又所以爲柔用，而元氣之所渾涵，時或有振而不靡。人見其張弛之交濟，而不知自其溫潤而栗者劑之也；人見其泰和而不偏，而不知本其純粹以精者出之也。謂之曰「剛柔節也」，豈惟无病於掩瑜而已哉？眞足以當玉鉉之實，而流光於无窮矣！然則爲人臣者，非相業之難，而相德之難；非相德之難，而協於中者難也。二聖交美而交發其義，有以哉！抑兩觀、三都之政，夾谷之役，蓋有時見其剛柔而未竟者，夫子寧无感也？周公至矣，雖然，以公玉鉉
translation_en: …and administration that is neither contentious nor hasty suffices to serve as a model for the states below, while the Nine Zones receive the vast blessings of his moistening grace. That the great enterprise is secure and the mandate of the cauldron (Ding) does not fail is because of this—both state and family are eternally trusted! That the pheasant fat is eaten and the contents of the cauldron are never exhausted is because of this—both reputation and position flourish together! Calling it "jade carrying-rings" and "great good fortune" and "advantageous"—how could this merely mean being free of anxiety over overturning the cauldron's food? Truly, he suffices to match the sovereign of the "golden carrying-rings" and hand down blessings for eternity! Then the Master [Confucius], on the basis of the loftiness of his achievements, traced them to his virtue, saying: "Firmness and softness are tempered in due measure." Thus, when one is lofty and bright yet prevails through softness, that prevailing is precisely what serves the use of firmness; as his spiritual vital energy unfolds, its movement seems bounded and never transgresses. When one is deep and reserved yet prevails through firmness, that prevailing is in turn what serves the use of softness; as his primordial vital energy encompasses all, at times it rouses itself and never flags. Others see the mutual reinforcement of his tension and relaxation, without knowing that it is tempered from that within him which is warm, lustrous, and yet firm; others see his great harmony without partiality, without knowing that it issues from his fundamental purity and refinement. Calling it "firmness and softness are tempered in due measure"—how could this merely mean having no flaw that obscures the luster of the jade? Truly, it suffices to match the reality of the jade carrying-rings and cast its radiance into infinity! This being so, for one who serves as a minister, it is not the achievements of a prime minister that are difficult, but the virtue of a prime minister that is difficult; and it is not the virtue of a prime minister that is difficult, but harmonizing with the mean that is difficult. That the two sages mutually praised and mutually elucidated its meaning—was there not good reason for it! Yet in the governance demonstrated at the Two Watchtowers and the Three Capitals, and in the encounter at Jiagu, there were times when his firmness and softness were manifested but not brought to full completion—how could the Master be without deep feeling over this? The Duke of Zhou was the ultimate! Even so, with the Duke's jade carrying-rings…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
之相功成而鴟鴞之詩作蓋几几焉故其象乾
上九曰亢龍有悔而夫子之賛用九曰天德不
可爲首也夫微伸其用於柔而深示其戒於亢
者所以安鼎鉉地也二聖之旨淵矣
有天地然後萬物生焉
熊夢祥
同考試官敎諭朱批發揮天地萬物理旣明暢詞亦
勁健可以式矣
同考試官學正蕭批純雅中有奇氣子蓋學于易而有
===
得者
考試官敎授黃批發然後字最明
考試官敎授郭批典實雅暢
觀天地之生乎物而易之首乾坤者可知矣蓋
天地羣物之祖也有天地而後有萬物乾坤爲
諸卦之首也宜哉且夫易不能外陰陽以爲卦
而乾坤其綱也物不能外陰陽以有生而天地
其統也觀卦序者即天地而乾坤可識矣何也
方太極未判之先无所謂天地亦无所謂萬物
punctuated:
之相，功成而《鴟鴞》之詩作，蓋几几焉。故其《象》乾上九曰：「亢龍有悔。」而夫子之賛用九曰：「天德不可爲首也。」夫微伸其用於柔，而深示其戒於亢者，所以安鼎鉉地也。二聖之旨淵矣。

有天地然後萬物生焉

熊夢祥

同考試官敎諭朱批：發揮天地萬物，理旣明暢，詞亦勁健，可以式矣。
同考試官學正蕭批：純雅中有奇氣，子蓋學于《易》而有得者。
考試官敎授黃批：發「然後」字最明。
考試官敎授郭批：典實雅暢。

觀天地之生乎物，而《易》之首乾、坤者可知矣。蓋天地，羣物之祖也。有天地而後有萬物，乾、坤爲諸卦之首也，宜哉！且夫《易》不能外陰陽以爲卦，而乾、坤其綱也；物不能外陰陽以有生，而天地其統也。觀卦序者，即天地而乾、坤可識矣。何也？方太極未判之先，无所謂天地，亦无所謂萬物
translation_en:
… ministry as a jade carrying-bar, when his achievements were complete, the ode "The Owl" (Chixiao) was composed, showing how composed and self-possessed he was. Thus, in his Line Statement for Top Nine of Qian, he said: "The arrogant dragon will have cause for regret." And the Master, in praising All Nines, said: "Heavenly virtue must not take the lead." Indeed, subtly extending its application through gentleness while deeply revealing its warning against arrogance is the way to secure the position of the cauldron's carrying-bar. Profound indeed is the meaning of the two sages!

"Only after there are heaven and earth are the myriad things born therein."

By Xiong Mengxiang 熊夢祥

Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Zhu comments: In expounding upon heaven, earth, and the myriad things, the reasoning is clear and fluent, and the diction is vigorous and strong; it can serve as a model.
Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Xiao comments: Within its purity and elegance there is an extraordinary vitality; you are surely one who has studied the Book of Changes (Yi) and gained insight from it.
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Huang comments: It brings out the meaning of the words "only after" (ranhou) most clearly.
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Guo comments: Classical, substantive, elegant, and fluent.

By observing how heaven and earth give birth to things, one can understand why the Book of Changes places Qian and Kun at the head. For heaven and earth are the ancestors of the multitude of things. Only after there are heaven and earth are there the myriad things; how fitting it is that Qian and Kun stand at the head of all the hexagrams! Moreover, the Changes cannot form hexagrams outside of yin and yang, and Qian and Kun are their guiding cord; things cannot come into life outside of yin and yang, and heaven and earth are their overarching unity. Those who observe the sequence of the hexagrams can look at heaven and earth and thereby understand Qian and Kun. Why is this? Before the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji) had divided, there was neither what is called heaven and earth, nor what is called the myriad things…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
也惟夫一元闢而清寧之奠位者肇兩間之化
育二氣分而易簡之成德者生羣物之散殊有
是天斯有是大生焉而高明之上覆固庶類之
所以資始有是地斯有是廣生焉而博厚之下
載固品彙之所以資生物必得理以成性而天
地者理之原也雖性命之各正萬有不齊而凡
有是性者孰非此生生之理以發育之耶物必
得氣以成形而天地者氣之宰也雖太和之保
合萬有不一而凡有是形者孰非此生生之氣
===
以楊詡之耶故自對待而言則天主其始地作
其成一之神者兩之所以化也而貞觀立生成
之本自流行而言則天道下濟地道上行兩之
化者一之所以神也而化醇顯絪縕之機要其
理天地不為先萬物不為後而稽其序不有天
地其何有萬物哉夫物不能不生於天地則易
不能不首乎乾坤矣聖人之序卦也有以夫甞
疑之萬物之生原于天地而天地又安從生耶
蓋自太極中來也太極者固天地之所以化生
punctuated: 也。惟夫一元闢而清寧之奠位者，肇兩間之化育；二氣分而易簡之成德者，生羣物之散殊。有是天，斯有是大生焉，而高明之上覆，固庶類之所以資始；有是地，斯有是廣生焉，而博厚之下載，固品彙之所以資生。物必得理以成性，而天地者，理之原也。雖性命之各正，萬有不齊，而凡有是性者，孰非此生生之理以發育之耶？物必得氣以成形，而天地者，氣之宰也。雖太和之保合，萬有不一，而凡有是形者，孰非此生生之氣以楊詡之耶？故自對待而言，則天主其始，地作其成，一之神者，兩之所以化也，而貞觀立生成之本；自流行而言，則天道下濟，地道上行，兩之化者，一之所以神也，而化醇顯絪縕之機。要其理，天地不為先，萬物不為後；而稽其序，不有天地，其何有萬物哉？夫物不能不生於天地，則易不能不首乎乾坤矣。聖人之序卦也，有以夫！甞疑之：萬物之生原于天地，而天地又安從生耶？蓋自太極中來也。太極者，固天地之所以化生
translation_en: … Only when the Primal Unity opened up, and that which is pure and tranquil settled into their positions, did the transformation and nourishment within the space between them begin; when the two vital forces separated, and that which is easy and simple perfected their virtues, the myriad things in their dispersed diversity were born. Only where there is this Heaven is there this great generation, and its lofty brilliance overarching from above is truly that from which the multitude of kinds draw their beginning; only where there is this Earth is there this broad generation, and its vast thickness supporting from below is truly that from which the various categories of beings draw their birth. Things must obtain principle in order to complete their nature, and Heaven and Earth are the source of principle. Although each thing rectifies its own nature and destiny in ten thousand unequal ways, among all that possess this nature, which is not developed and nourished by this principle of ceaseless generation? Things must obtain vital force in order to form their physical shapes, and Heaven and Earth are the rulers of vital force. Although Supreme Harmony is preserved in union across ten thousand diverse beings, among all that possess this form, which is not animated and breathed into life [?] by this vital force of ceaseless generation? Therefore, speaking in terms of their complementary opposition, Heaven presides over the beginning and Earth brings about the completion: the unfathomable wonder of the One is that by which the Two transform, and their constant manifestation establishes the foundation of generation and completion. Speaking in terms of their developmental flow, the Way of Heaven descends to aid and the Way of Earth ascends to act: the transformation of the Two is that by which the One works its unfathomable wonder, and their purifying transformation reveals the mechanism of generative intertwining. Summing up the fundamental principle, Heaven and Earth are not prior and the myriad things are not posterior; yet examining their sequence, if there were no Heaven and Earth, how could there be the myriad things? Since things cannot but be born from Heaven and Earth, the Book of Changes (Yi) cannot but begin with Qian and Kun. When the sage ordered the hexagrams, he had good reason indeed! Yet one might wonder: the birth of the myriad things originates in Heaven and Earth, but from where, then, are Heaven and Earth born? They come from the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji). The Supreme Ultimate is truly that by which Heaven and Earth transform and generate …

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
萬物而乾坤之所以變而爲六十四卦者也識
其妙則易即我我即易而天地位萬物育又安
能有外於此者哉是故善學易者求諸吾之心
極而後可
書
學于古訓乃有獲
秦嵩
同考試官學正趙批理明詞暢而意亦懇到
同考試官敎授周批發明反己之學甚善亦學之有
===
獲者錄之
考試官敎授黄批思婉詞達
考試官敎授郭批得傅說納誨意
大臣啓賢王以學古之益欲其求諸己也蓋理
莫備于古訓也學之斯有自得之益矣而何以
多聞爲哉賢王宜知反求矣傅說之意若曰訓
志之義固臣職之當供而反己之學實君道之
當勉王之欲建事也可徒求多聞哉彼脩身治
天下其事行之古人其理載於古訓不有以學
punctuated:
萬物，而乾坤之所以變而爲六十四卦者也。識其妙，則《易》即我、我即《易》，而天地位、萬物育，又安能有外於此者哉？是故善學《易》者，求諸吾之心極而後可。

《書》
「學于古訓乃有獲。」
秦嵩
同考試官學正趙批：理明詞暢，而意亦懇到。
同考試官敎授周批：發明反己之學甚善，亦學之有獲者，錄之。
考試官敎授黄批：思婉詞達。
考試官敎授郭批：得傅說納誨意。

大臣啓賢王以學古之益，欲其求諸己也。蓋理莫備于古訓也，學之斯有自得之益矣，而何以多聞爲哉？賢王宜知反求矣。傅說之意若曰：訓志之義，固臣職之當供；而反己之學，實君道之當勉。王之欲建事也，可徒求多聞哉？彼脩身、治天下，其事行之古人，其理載於古訓，不有以學
translation_en:
… all things, and whereby Qian and Kun transform to become the sixty-four hexagrams. If one grasps this subtlety, then the Book of Changes (Yi) is oneself, and oneself is the Book of Changes; how could the proper placement of Heaven and Earth and the nourishment of all things lie outside of this? Therefore, one who is good at studying the Book of Changes must first seek it in the Supreme Ultimate of one's own mind.

Book of Documents (Shu)
"By studying the ancient lessons, one truly achieves attainment."
Qin Song 秦嵩
Associate Examiner Department Director of Schools Zhao 趙 comments: The principles are clear, the diction is fluent, and the meaning is earnest and thorough.
Associate Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Zhou 周 comments: It elucidates the learning of self-reflection very well; the author is himself one who has achieved attainment through study. Record it.
Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Huang 黄 comments: The thought is subtle and the expression is articulate.
Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Guo 郭 comments: It captures the intention of Fu Yue 傅說 in offering counsel.

When the great minister enlightened the worthy king regarding the benefits of studying antiquity, he wished him to seek it within himself. For principle is nowhere more complete than in the ancient lessons; when one studies them, there is the benefit of personal realization—what need is there merely for wide hearing? The worthy king ought to know to turn inward and seek it in himself. The meaning of Fu Yue was as if to say: The duty of instructing your will is indeed what a minister's office ought to provide, yet the learning of self-reflection is truly what the Way of the ruler ought to strive after. In Your Majesty's desire to establish great undertakings, how can you merely seek wide hearing? As for cultivating the self and governing the world, those affairs were practiced by the ancients, and their principles are recorded in the ancient lessons. If one does not have the means to study…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
之孰從而得之誠能不以罔顯者諉之已而好
古敏求之力亹亹勿忘不以交脩者資諸人而
多識蓄德之功孜孜匪懈以懋聖脩之極則于
古脩身之訓學之理無窮功亦無間而欽聖謨
以裕明哲者析之精也以弘錫類之化則于古
治天下之訓學之理愈備功亦愈密而遵王道
以廣作則者合之大也誠若是也將見探討之
既精則古訓之理與吾人相浹洽而資深逢原
之有機緝熈之罔間則古人之心與我心相感
===
孚而融會貫通之無外自其學脩身而明哲之
體吾其立之無俟朝夕之納誨而日新之盛德
不本之舊章而有餘乎自其學治天下而作則
之用吾其具之非必左右之啓沃而富有之大
業不監之成憲而自裕乎至是則理無不明事
無不建有不終於罔顯者矣學古之益如此吾
王尚反而求之抑帝王之學心學也始而學古
學此理于心也既而有獲獲此理于心也由是
而乃來而積躬而罔覺何莫非此心此理之貫
punctuated: 之，孰從而得之？誠能不以罔顯者諉之已，而好古敏求之力，亹亹勿忘；不以交脩者資諸人，而多識蓄德之功，孜孜匪懈。以懋聖脩之極，則于古脩身之訓學之，理無窮，功亦無間，而欽聖謨以裕明哲者，析之精也；以弘錫類之化，則于古治天下之訓學之，理愈備，功亦愈密，而遵王道以廣作則者，合之大也。誠若是也，將見探討之既精，則古訓之理與吾人相浹洽，而資深逢原之有機；緝熈之罔間，則古人之心與我心相感孚，而融會貫通之無外。自其學脩身，而明哲之體吾其立之，無俟朝夕之納誨，而日新之盛德，不本之舊章而有餘乎？自其學治天下，而作則之用吾其具之，非必左右之啓沃，而富有之大業，不監之成憲而自裕乎？至是則理無不明，事無不建，有不終於罔顯者矣。學古之益如此，吾王尚反而求之！抑帝王之學，心學也。始而學古，學此理于心也；既而有獲，獲此理于心也。由是而乃來、而積躬、而罔覺，何莫非此心此理之貫
translation_en: … it, how could one attain it? If Your Majesty can truly refrain from excusing yourself on account of what is not yet manifest to you, and instead tirelessly maintain the effort of loving antiquity and earnestly seeking it; and refrain from merely relying on others for mutual cultivation, and instead diligently and unremittingly apply the effort of remembering much to store up virtue: then, to strive for the pinnacle of sagely self-cultivation, you will study the ancient teachings on cultivating the person—as their principles are inexhaustible, your effort will likewise be unceasing, and by revering the counsels of the sages to enrich your明哲 (clear-sighted wisdom), you will analyze them with precision. And to broaden the transformative influence that bestows goodness on all your kind, you will study the ancient teachings on governing the world—as their principles are ever more complete, your effort will likewise be ever more meticulous, and by following the Kingly Way to extend your role as a model, you will synthesize them on a grand scale. If it is truly like this, one will see that once your investigation and inquiry have become refined, the principles of the ancient teachings will thoroughly saturate your being, giving rise to the vital dynamic of drawing deeply from them and encountering their source everywhere; and once your bright, continuous effort is without interruption, the minds of the ancients and your own mind will mutually resonate in trust, achieving a comprehensive and seamless integration with nothing left outside. From studying how to cultivate the person, the substance of clear-sighted wisdom will be established by oneself; without waiting for morning and evening admonitions and instructions, will not the flourishing virtue of daily renewal be grounded in the ancient statutes and have more than enough to spare? From studying how to govern the world, the function of serving as a model will be fully present in oneself; without necessarily relying on the enlightening guidance of your attendants, will not the great enterprise of abundant possession take the established constitutions as its mirror and be naturally ample? Reaching this point, there will be no principle left unclarified and no affair left unestablished, and you will surely not end in remaining unmanifest! Such are the benefits of studying antiquity; may my King turn within and seek them! Moreover, the learning of emperors and kings is the learning of the mind-and-heart (xinxue). At the beginning, in studying antiquity, one studies this principle within the mind; afterward, in gaining something from it, one gains this principle within the mind. From this, its coming spontaneously, its accumulation in one's own person, and its occurring without even being conscious of it—what among these is not the thoroughgoing…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
徵乎以此論學而輔德高宗所以爲商令主也
宜後世誦中興之烈而稱傅說之功不衰
聰明齊聖小大之臣咸懷忠良其侍御僕
從罔匪正人以旦夕承弼厥辟
李際春
同考試官學正趙批理致精深詞意懇切善發周王
責望近臣之意
同考試官教授周批詞氣渾融冲然古調
考試官教授黄批懇切有裨治道非苟作者
===
考試官教授郭批詞贍意婉
聖世君臣合德而猶資於近臣之輔焉甚矣輔
相有關於君德也以文武明良之盛且於近臣
有資焉而况於後王也乎昔穆王命伯冏之意
若曰君心係於所養故親賢急矣近臣要焉吾
嘗稽諸先王而知其然矣彼文武之君何君也
聰明齊聖之資創述其重光焉作哲作謀而有
敬有臨君則天下之聖君也文武之臣何臣也
忠正純良之志小大其咸懷焉師師在列而濟
punctuated:
徵乎？以此論學而輔德，高宗所以爲商令主也。宜後世誦中興之烈，而稱傅說之功不衰。

聰明齊聖，小大之臣咸懷忠良；其侍御僕從，罔匪正人，以旦夕承弼厥辟。
李際春
同考試官學正趙批：理致精深，詞意懇切，善發周王責望近臣之意。
同考試官教授周批：詞氣渾融，冲然古調。
考試官教授黄批：懇切有裨治道，非苟作者。
考試官教授郭批：詞贍意婉。

聖世君臣合德，而猶資於近臣之輔焉。甚矣，輔相有關於君德也！以文、武明良之盛，且於近臣有資焉，而况於後王也乎？昔穆王命伯冏之意，若曰：君心係於所養，故親賢急矣，近臣要焉。吾嘗稽諸先王而知其然矣。彼文、武之君，何君也？聰明齊聖之資，創述其重光焉；作哲作謀，而有敬有臨，君則天下之聖君也。文、武之臣，何臣也？忠正純良之志，小大其咸懷焉；師師在列，而濟
translation_en:
…manifestation? Discussing learning and assisting virtue in this way is how Gaozong (高宗) became an exemplary ruler of the Shang dynasty. Fittingly, later generations have extolled the splendor of his dynastic revival and praised the achievements of Fu Yue (傅說) without cease.

"Intelligent, discerning, and sagely, their ministers, great and small, all cherished loyalty and goodness. Their attendants, grooms, and followers were none other than upright men, who morning and evening assisted their sovereign." [Book of Documents, "Charge to Jiong" (囧命)]
Li Jichun (李際春)
Comment by Associate Examiner Department Director of Schools Zhao: The reasoning is profound and the expression and intent are earnest; it skillfully brings out the King of Zhou's intention in placing expectations on his close attendants.
Comment by Associate Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Zhou: The diction and spirit are harmonious and integrated, serenely carrying an ancient tone.
Comment by Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Huang: Earnest and beneficial to the way of governance; not the work of a careless writer.
Comment by Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Guo: Rich in diction and graceful in meaning.

In a sagely age, ruler and ministers were united in virtue, and yet they still relied on the assistance of close attendants. Profound indeed is the bearing that assistance and counsel have upon a ruler's virtue! When even at the height of enlightened rulers and worthy ministers under Kings Wen and Wu they relied upon close attendants, how much more so must later kings? In the past, the gist of King Mu's (穆王) charge to Bo Jiong (伯冏) was as if to say: The ruler's mind depends on how it is nourished; therefore, drawing close to the worthy is urgent, and close attendants are vital. I have examined this in light of the former kings and know it to be so. What manner of rulers were those kings, Wen and Wu? With endowments of intelligence, discernment, and sageliness, in founding and continuing the dynasty they shone with redoubled brilliance; showing wisdom and resourcefulness, possessing reverence and majesty in overseeing the realm, as rulers they were the sagely rulers of the world. What manner of ministers were the ministers of Wen and Wu? Aspirations of loyalty, uprightness, purity, and goodness were cherished by great and small alike; emulating one another in the ranks of office and harmoniously…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
濟同心臣則天下之賢臣也宜若無藉於近臣
之助矣然而在文武也不以廟堂有正人而忽
其近侍之選故侍御僕從人不一也而罔非庶
常吉士之流在近臣也不以大庭有顯諫而忘
乎承弼之忠故旦夕之際時不同也而常効引
君當道之益慮聰明之自用而侃侃正倫日敷
陳於讌閒之間或以將順或以匡救即其心一
大臣忠良之心也而孰有眩之以非禮者哉慮
齊聖之自賢而亹亹忠言時賛襄於游息之際
===
或獻其可或替其否即其心一小臣忠良之心
也而孰有導之以非辟者哉夫以文武之君臣
而有賴於近臣如此則爲之後者可知矣冏爲
太僕尚知所以慎其選哉抑人君之德動息有
養而燕僻之地漸染尤深茍君德有虧於宮禁
之中而欲轉移於殿陛之上計亦晚矣綴衣虎
賁周公於成王屢致意焉老成謀國其遠慮類
如此噫穆王之命伯冏亦諄諄矣而車轍馬跡
徧於天下曾未聞近臣有匡弼者豈伯冏不能
punctuated: 濟同心，臣則天下之賢臣也。宜若無藉於近臣之助矣。然而在文武也，不以廟堂有正人而忽其近侍之選，故侍御僕從，人不一也，而罔非庶常吉士之流；在近臣也，不以大庭有顯諫而忘乎承弼之忠，故旦夕之際，時不同也，而常効引君當道之益。慮聰明之自用，而侃侃正倫，日敷陳於讌閒之間，或以將順，或以匡救，即其心一，大臣忠良之心也，而孰有眩之以非禮者哉？慮齊聖之自賢，而亹亹忠言，時賛襄於游息之際，或獻其可，或替其否，即其心一，小臣忠良之心也，而孰有導之以非辟者哉？夫以文武之君臣，而有賴於近臣如此，則爲之後者可知矣。冏爲太僕，尚知所以慎其選哉！」抑人君之德，動息有養，而燕僻之地，漸染尤深。茍君德有虧於宮禁之中，而欲轉移於殿陛之上，計亦晚矣。綴衣、虎賁，周公於成王屢致意焉，老成謀國，其遠慮類如此。噫！穆王之命伯冏亦諄諄矣，而車轍馬跡徧於天下，曾未聞近臣有匡弼者，豈伯冏不能
translation_en:
…and in dignified harmony they were of one mind—the ministers were thus the worthiest ministers in the world. It would seem as if they had no need for the assistance of close attendants. And yet, on the part of Kings Wen and Wu, they did not neglect the selection of their personal attendants just because there were upright men in the court; therefore, among their attendants, drivers, and personal servants, though the individuals were varied, there was none who was not of the caliber of a Cultivated and Constant Auspicious Gentleman (shuchang jishi). On the part of the close attendants, they did not forget their loyalty in assisting and correcting the ruler just because there was open remonstrance in the grand court; therefore, morning and evening, though the occasions differed, they constantly rendered the benefit of guiding the ruler toward the proper Way. Lest the kings rely solely on their own intelligence and discernment, with forthrightness and proper principles they daily set forth counsel during moments of leisure and repose—sometimes to comply with and further their goodness, sometimes to rectify and rescue them from error. Their hearts were identical with the loyal and virtuous hearts of the great ministers; who among them, then, would dazzle the ruler with what is contrary to ritual propriety? Lest the kings, in their solemnity and sageliness, consider themselves self-sufficiently worthy, with tireless words of loyalty they constantly assisted them during times of recreation and rest—sometimes offering what was acceptable, sometimes dissuading them from what was objectionable. Their hearts were identical with the loyal and virtuous hearts of the lesser ministers; who among them, then, would lead the ruler into depravity and perversity? Now, if such sovereigns and ministers as Kings Wen and Wu relied upon their close attendants to this degree, then how much more so for those who come after them can well be known! As Director of the Imperial Stud (Taipu), may you, Jiong, know how to be cautious in their selection!"

Furthermore, the virtue of a ruler is cultivated in both activity and rest, and in places of private leisure and seclusion, the gradual influence of his surroundings goes especially deep. If the ruler's virtue suffers a deficit within the palace precincts, and one wishes to turn it around before the steps of the throne hall, the plan is already too late. Keepers of the Robes (Zhuiyi) and Brave Rapid-as-Tigers Guardsmen (Huben) were subjects to which the Duke of Zhou repeatedly directed his attention when instructing King Cheng; when experienced elders plan for the state, their far-reaching foresight is generally like this. Alas! King Mu's charge to Bo Jiong was also earnest and repeated, yet his chariot tracks and horse hoofprints covered the entire realm, and one never heard of his close attendants offering rectification or assistance. Could it be that Bo Jiong was unable to…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
率其職歟無惑乎文武之業之不振也
詩
鶴鳴于九皐聲聞于天魚在于渚或潜在
淵樂彼之園爰有樹檀其下維穀他山
之石可以攻玉
李宗魯
同考試官教諭殷批〔順題發揮得諷諫體〕
同考試官教諭鍾批〔諷言須含蓄最難體會此作思〕
〔婉而義雋有味乎其言之也宜錄以式〕
===
考試官教授黃批〔意完詞雅〕
考試官教授郭批〔可與言詩者〕
詩人再托物以諷君而其義為益精也蓋誠明
好惡君道也取諸物有餘諷焉為此詩者其知
道乎且夫臣子之事君不難於納誨而善用其
誨之為難鶴鳴詩人蓋有以識此矣故其詞又
若曰善比類者必以物善觀物者必以道天下
之物理無窮也請得為王言之鶴之鳴也于彼
九皐若幽遠而不可即矣而其聲則不惟聞于
punctuated:
率其職歟？無惑乎文武之業之不振也。
詩
「鶴鳴于九皐，聲聞于天。魚在于渚，或潜在淵。樂彼之園，爰有樹檀，其下維穀。他山之石，可以攻玉。」
李宗魯
同考試官教諭殷批：〔順題發揮，得諷諫體。〕
同考試官教諭鍾批：〔諷言須含蓄，最難體會。此作思〕〔婉而義雋，有味乎其言之也，宜錄以式。〕
考試官教授黃批：〔意完詞雅。〕
考試官教授郭批：〔可與言詩者。〕
詩人再托物以諷君，而其義為益精也。蓋誠明、好惡，君道也，取諸物有餘諷焉。為此詩者，其知道乎！且夫臣子之事君，不難於納誨，而善用其誨之為難。《鶴鳴》詩人，蓋有以識此矣。故其詞又若曰：善比類者必以物，善觀物者必以道。天下之物理無窮也，請得為王言之。鶴之鳴也，于彼九皐，若幽遠而不可即矣，而其聲則不惟聞于
translation_en:
… fulfill his duties? It is no wonder that the enterprise of Kings Wen and Wu failed to revive.

Classic of Poetry (Shijing)
"The crane cries in the nine marshes, and its voice is heard in the heavens. The fish is by the islet, or plunges into the deep. Pleasant is that garden, where there are sandalwood trees, and beneath them is the paper-mulberry. The stones of other hills may be used to polish jade."

Li Zonglu
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Yin comments: 〔Develops the theme smoothly and captures the style of indirect remonstrance.〕
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Zhong comments: 〔Words of indirect remonstrance must be reserved and implicit, which is most difficult to grasp. This essay is subtle in thought and incisive in meaning; there is true flavor in its words. It should be recorded as a model.〕
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Huang comments: 〔The meaning is complete and the diction elegant.〕
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Guo comments: 〔One with whom one can speak of the Odes.〕

The poet once again uses things as allegories to remonstrate indirectly with his ruler, and his meaning becomes all the more refined. Indeed, sincerity, enlightenment, likes, and dislikes constitute the Way of the ruler; drawing analogies from things provides ample indirect admonition. He who composed this ode truly understood the Way! Moreover, when a subject serves his ruler, the difficulty lies not in offering instruction, but in skillfully applying that instruction. The poet of "The Crane Cries" (Heming) surely understood this. Thus his words continue as if to say: He who excels at drawing analogies must use things, and he who excels at observing things must use the Way. The principles of things in the world are inexhaustible; allow me to speak of them for the King. When the crane cries in those nine marshes, it seems secluded, distant, and unreachable, yet its voice is heard not only in…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
野而聞于天焉顯微無間雖鶴不得而秘之也
誠之不可掩如此而豈惟鶴哉魚之在于渚也
自淵而出若有迹而可見矣而其潜又在于淵
而不專於渚焉兩在不測雖魚不得而知之也
機之不可執如此而豈惟魚哉園有樹檀不但
下維籜也穀不可以爲檀而檀下生之可樂者
有可憎焉愛檀而忘其下之穀豈善用愛者乎
而天下之類於檀者尚多也他山之石不但可
爲錯也石不可以爲玉而攻玉取之可棄者有
可愛焉惡石而忘其玉之攻豈善用惡者乎而
天下之類於石者尚多也吾王誠能反觀於身
引伸於類即鶴鳴而進於誠矣即魚躍而進於
明矣即好惡之必察而進於公矣致治保邦寧
有窮乎意詩人可謂微而婉忠而誨者矣雖然
誠明好惡皆道也而要之則本於誠焉蓋惟誠
則明明則通惟誠則公公則普而天德王道備
矣詩人首舉以爲言不既深乎否則中無定主
何取於淵魚之察而任賢反貳去邪反疑將有
punctuated: 野，而聞于天焉。顯微無間，雖鶴不得而秘之也。誠之不可掩如此，而豈惟鶴哉？魚之在于渚也，自淵而出，若有迹而可見矣；而其潜又在于淵，而不專於渚焉。兩在不測，雖魚不得而知之也。機之不可執如此，而豈惟魚哉？園有樹檀，不但下維籜也。穀不可以爲檀，而檀下生之，可樂者有可憎焉。愛檀而忘其下之穀，豈善用愛者乎？而天下之類於檀者尚多也。他山之石，不但可爲錯也。石不可以爲玉，而攻玉取之，可棄者有可愛焉。惡石而忘其玉之攻，豈善用惡者乎？而天下之類於石者尚多也。吾王誠能反觀於身，引伸於類，即鶴鳴而進於誠矣，即魚躍而進於明矣，即好惡之必察而進於公矣，致治保邦寧有窮乎？意詩人可謂微而婉、忠而誨者矣。雖然，誠明好惡皆道也，而要之則本於誠焉。蓋惟誠則明，明則通；惟誠則公，公則普，而天德王道備矣。詩人首舉以爲言，不既深乎？否則中無定主，何取於淵魚之察？而任賢反貳，去邪反疑，將有
translation_en: … the wilds, it is even heard in Heaven. Between the manifest and the subtle there is no gap; even the crane cannot keep it secret. Such is the impossibility of concealing sincerity—and is this true only of the crane? When the fish is by the islet, emerging from the deep, it seems to leave traces that can be seen; yet when it dives, it is back in the deep and does not stay exclusively by the islet. Present in both places unfathomably, even the fish itself cannot know it. Such is the impossibility of grasping the subtle springs of things—and is this true only of the fish? In the garden stand planted sandalwood trees, and beneath them are not merely fallen leaves. The paper-mulberry cannot be counted as sandalwood, yet it grows beneath the sandalwood; thus within what is delightful there is something detestable. To love the sandalwood while forgetting the paper-mulberry beneath it—how could that be knowing how to apply one's love well? And in the world there are still many things like the sandalwood. The stones of other hills can serve not merely as grindstones. Stone cannot be counted as jade, yet it is taken to polish jade; thus within what might be discarded there is something lovable. To dislike the stone while forgetting that it polishes jade—how could that be knowing how to apply one's dislike well? And in the world there are still many things like the stone. If our King can truly reflect upon his own person and extend the analogy to other categories—advancing in sincerity from the crane's cry, advancing in discernment from the leaping of the fish, and advancing in impartiality from the necessary examination of likes and dislikes—then how could there be any limit to achieving good governance and preserving the state? Indeed, the poet may be called subtle and gentle, loyal and instructive! Even so, sincerity, discernment, and proper likes and dislikes are all part of the Way, yet in essence they are rooted in sincerity. For only when there is sincerity is there discernment, and with discernment comes comprehension; only when there is sincerity is there impartiality, and with impartiality comes universality—and thus Heavenly virtue and the Kingly Way are complete. That the poet raised this first in his words—is its meaning not profound? Otherwise, with no fixed ruler within one's heart, what use would there be in peering after fish in the abyss? In employing the worthy one would instead harbor doubts, and in removing the wicked one would instead hesitate; there would soon be …

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
伐檀之詠履石之譏矣豈詩人托物意哉故君
子誠之爲貴
日就月將學有緝煕于光明佛時仔肩示
我顯德行
李登
同考試官教諭殷批懋學資臣成王所以圖鴻業也
子晰其旨若於今有餘望焉豈直文辭爾雅哉取之
同考試官教諭鍾批講成王勉敬求助處甚懇切
考試官教授黃批原天命敬德胃之極是
===
考試官教授郭批精純典則儘有古意錄之
賢王勉純敬之學而因求助於臣焉夫人巳交
脩聖學之全功也賢王以之聖敬其庶幾乎成
王受羣臣之戒而述其言曰敬者帝王之心法
也心之體本極其光明而敬之入莫先於德行
顧其責在我而交脩之益不能不資諸人耳是
故惟予小子不敢以不聰之質自諉也必思予
之事天以心而事心以敬也其爲力誠不易也
凡所以勅天之命惟時惟幾者常亹亹焉日有
punctuated:
伐檀之詠、履石之譏矣，豈詩人托物意哉？故君子誠之爲貴。

日就月將，學有緝煕于光明。佛時仔肩，示我顯德行。
李登

賢王勉純敬之學，而因求助於臣焉。夫人巳交脩，聖學之全功也，賢王以之，聖敬其庶幾乎！成王受羣臣之戒而述其言，曰：敬者，帝王之心法也。心之體本極其光明，而敬之入莫先於德行。顧其責在我，而交脩之益不能不資諸人耳。是故惟予小子，不敢以不聰之質自諉也，必思予之事天以心，而事心以敬也，其爲力誠不易也。凡所以勅天之命，惟時惟幾者，常亹亹焉。日有
translation_en:
… the chanting of "Cutting the Sandalwood" (Fa tan) and the ridicule of "Treading on the Stones." How could that be the poet's intention in using metaphors from things? Therefore, the gentleman holds sincerity to be most precious.

"With daily accomplishment and monthly progress, may my learning have continuous brightness unto illumination. Assist me in bearing this heavy burden on my shoulders, and show me glorious virtuous conduct."
Li Deng 李登

Associate Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Yin comments: Striving in learning and relying on his ministers—this was how King Cheng planned for his great enterprise. You have elucidated its meaning as if holding abundant hopes for the present day; how is this merely a matter of refined and elegant diction! Selected.
Associate Examiner, Instructor Zhong comments: The exposition of where King Cheng strives for reverence and seeks assistance is deeply earnest.
Examiner, Professor (jiaoshou) Huang comments: Tracing the Mandate of Heaven and revering virtue to introduce it [? 胃之, likely for 冒之] is utterly right.
Examiner, Professor Guo comments: Pure, refined, and observant of classical standards, thoroughly possessing an ancient spirit. Recorded.

The worthy king strives in the learning of pure reverence, and thereby seeks assistance from his ministers. Now, mutual cultivation between others and oneself is the complete work of sage learning; since the worthy king practiced this, did he not come close to sage reverence! King Cheng received the admonitions of his assembled ministers and recounted their words, saying: Reverence is the method of the mind of emperors and kings. The substance of the mind is originally supremely luminous, and for entering into reverence, nothing takes precedence over virtuous conduct. Yet while the responsibility lies with me, for the benefit of mutual cultivation I cannot but rely upon others. Therefore, I, the little child, dare not excuse myself on account of my unintelligent nature; I must reflect that I serve Heaven with my mind, and manage my mind with reverence—and the effort required for this is truly not easy. In all whereby I cautiously attend to the Mandate of Heaven at every moment and in the subtlest beginnings, I am constantly tireless. Each day there is…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
所就功不間於日矣而又緝而熙之以底于純
粹之精月有所將功無忘於月矣而又續而明
之以造于聖脩之極庶幾吾心之天與在天之
天光明而無間斯已焉此固予之不敢不勉者
也而豈予一人之可易能哉惟汝諸臣亦無以
不聰之質而棄予也尚念予之所履天位而所
學天德也為任誠至重也凡可以為予之助啓
心沃心者日諄諄焉戒之以敬天未已也而復
示以入德之方俾就將者有所持循啓之以保
===
命未已也而又詔之顯德之行俾緝熙者有所
依據庶幾純天之德與繼天之任克勝而無忝
斯已焉此固予之所望于羣臣者也汝羣臣其
尚憫予哉噫成王之疾敬厥德可謂至矣玆其
所以能宥密基命緝熙殫心而為有周之令主
歟大抵敬者文武傳心之要而天命自敕交警
於上下之間尤虞廷君臣之休風也成王以幼
冲蒞政而於此倦倦焉可不謂賢乎然不有寅
畏忱恂之訓或亦無以進於是者故敬以格天
punctuated: 所就，功不間於日矣，而又緝而熙之，以底于純粹之精；月有所將，功無忘於月矣，而又續而明之，以造于聖脩之極。庶幾吾心之天與在天之天，光明而無間，斯已焉。此固予之不敢不勉者也，而豈予一人之可易能哉？惟汝諸臣亦無以不聰之質而棄予也，尚念予之所履天位而所學天德也，為任誠至重也。凡可以為予之助、啓心沃心者，日諄諄焉：戒之以敬天未已也，而復示以入德之方，俾就將者有所持循；啓之以保命未已也，而又詔之顯德之行，俾緝熙者有所依據。庶幾純天之德與繼天之任，克勝而無忝，斯已焉。此固予之所望于羣臣者也，汝羣臣其尚憫予哉！」噫！成王之疾敬厥德，可謂至矣。玆其所以能宥密基命、緝熙殫心，而為有周之令主歟！大抵敬者，文、武傳心之要；而天命自敕，交警於上下之間，尤虞廷君臣之休風也。成王以幼冲蒞政，而於此倦倦焉，可不謂賢乎？然不有寅畏忱恂之訓，或亦無以進於是者。故敬以格天，
translation_en:
…achieved daily, my effort never ceases for a day, and yet I continue and brighten it so as to reach the essence of pure perfection; and with progress made monthly, my effort is never forgotten for a month, and yet I carry on and illuminate it so as to attain the utmost of sagely self-cultivation. Only when the Heaven within my mind and the Heaven above are both luminous and without gap shall I stop. This is certainly what I dare not fail to strive for, yet how could I, one man alone, easily accomplish it? May all you ministers likewise not abandon me because of my unintelligent nature! Rather, bear in mind that what I occupy is the Heavenly position and what I study is Heavenly virtue, so that my responsibility is truly of the utmost weight. In all that can assist me by opening and enriching my mind, be earnest day by day: do not stop at admonishing me to revere Heaven, but further show me the way to enter into virtue, so that in my daily achievement and monthly progress I have something to hold to and follow; do not stop at instructing me to preserve the Mandate, but further counsel me in the conduct of manifest virtue, so that in my continuing and brightening I have something to rely upon. Only when I can bear the pure virtue of Heaven and the responsibility of succeeding to Heaven without disgrace shall I stop. This is certainly what I hope for from my ministers—may all you ministers take pity on me!”

Ah! King Cheng’s urgency in revering his virtue may be called supreme. Is this not why he was able to establish the Mandate in quietude and profundity, exhaust his mind in continuing luminosity, and become an admirable ruler of the Zhou dynasty? Broadly speaking, reverence is the essential teaching transmitted from mind to mind by Kings Wen and Wu; and admonishing oneself regarding the Mandate of Heaven, with ruler and ministers mutually cautioning one another above and below, was especially the fine custom of the sovereign and ministers at the court of Yu [Shun]. For King Cheng to have assumed governance in his youth and yet to have been so earnestly devoted to this—can he not be called worthy? Still, had there not been the instructions on reverent awe and sincere trustworthiness, perhaps he too would have had no means to advance to this state. Therefore, to reach Heaven through reverence…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
君道也敬以格君臣道也圖治者審諸
春秋
八月公會齊侯宋公鄭伯曹伯邾人于檉
僖公元年
周弘禴
同考試官教諭左批詳於當時事勢且融會二傳意簡明可録
考試官教授黃批發振威勤鄭意精切明當
考試官教授郭批縝密簡古氣味冲然
===
春秋紀內外之好而與伯者勤安攘之義也此
檉之役齊桓致勤於鄭以振中夏之威也春秋
所以與之耶昔楚以即齊之故仇鄭齊桓謀救
之是以有于檉之會魯之不誠罪也而獨與夫
桓者何蓋伯者之主夏盟也勤以恤患則威怠
以棄義則無震楚成浸强凌蔑中夏桓不起而
圖之其何以宗諸侯矣幸而齊桓糾合列辟念
彼懿親之患其義不可棄也而徵會以急其病
揆之中國之樞其勢不可失也而厚集以示之
punctuated:
君道也；敬以格君，臣道也。圖治者審諸！

《春秋》
「八月，公會齊侯、宋公、鄭伯、曹伯、邾人于檉。」〔僖公元年〕
周弘禴
同考試官教諭左批：詳於當時事勢，且融會二傳，意簡明可録。
考試官教授黃批：發振威勤鄭意，精切明當。
考試官教授郭批：縝密簡古，氣味冲然。

《春秋》紀內外之好，而與伯者勤安攘之義也。此檉之役，齊桓致勤於鄭，以振中夏之威也，《春秋》所以與之耶？昔楚以即齊之故仇鄭，齊桓謀救之，是以有于檉之會。魯之不誠，罪也，而獨與夫桓者何？蓋伯者之主夏盟也，勤以恤患則威，怠以棄義則無震。楚成浸强，凌蔑中夏，桓不起而圖之，其何以宗諸侯矣？幸而齊桓糾合列辟，念彼懿親之患，其義不可棄也，而徵會以急其病；揆之中國之樞，其勢不可失也，而厚集以示之
translation_en:
… is the Way of the ruler; to move the ruler through reverence is the Way of the minister. Let those who plan for good governance examine this carefully!

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"In the eighth month, the Duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, and a man of Zhu at Cheng." [First year of Duke Xi]

By Zhou Hongyue 周弘禴.
Associate Examiner Zuo, Instructor, comments: Well-informed on the circumstances of the time, and blending the two commentaries harmoniously; the ideas are concise and clear, worthy of recording.
Examiner Huang, Professor, comments: Develops the idea of rousing prestige and laboring on behalf of Zheng in a precise, incisive, clear, and fitting manner.
Examiner Guo, Professor, comments: Meticulous, concise, and ancient in style, with a serene and harmonious air.

When the Spring and Autumn Annals records amicable relations between the interior and the exterior, it approves of the hegemon's diligence in the duty of pacifying the interior and repelling the exterior. In this campaign at Cheng, Duke Huan of Qi (Qi Huan 齊桓) exerted himself on behalf of Zheng in order to rouse the prestige of the central Hua states. Is this not why the Spring and Autumn Annals approves of him? Formerly, because Zheng had aligned itself with Qi, Chu treated Zheng as an enemy. Duke Huan of Qi planned to rescue it, and therefore there was the meeting at Cheng. That Lu was insincere was a fault, yet why does it solely approve of Huan? For when a hegemon presides over the covenants of the Hua states, if he is diligent in relieving distress, he commands prestige; if he is negligent and abandons righteousness, he inspires no awe. As King Cheng of Chu (Chu Cheng 楚成) gradually grew strong and bullied and disdained the central Hua states, had Huan not risen to take countermeasures against him, how could he have served as the leader of the feudal lords? Fortunately, Duke Huan of Qi rallied the various rulers. Mindful of the distress of that close royal relative [Zheng], he saw that in righteousness it could not be abandoned, and so he summoned a meeting to urgently address its affliction; assessing it as the pivot of the Central States, he saw that its strategic position could not be lost, and so he assembled in force to display his…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
威簡書之急雖不卽及於鄭然而形禁勢格使
自爲解者桓其慮之深矣撻伐之威雖不卽懲
於荊然而經營圖合戢而時動者桓其籌之審
矣折衝於壇坫之上而仗義以遺諸姬之安異
日孔叔完守度德而不忍棄者非以齊有勤我
之力與不然鄭患方棘能不遄其南向之轍耶
指顧於俎豆之間而先聲以摧江漢之焰異日
屈完納款徼好而惟恐後者非以齊有制彼之
慮與不然楚氛方惡能遽遏其北方之圖耶故
===
兹會也在魯人敗邾之師有愆義干盟之咎而
齊桓謀鄭之念爲安夏攘夷之勤是故紀會以
美之而魯之罪比事見矣抑楚師三至而齊救
不至惡在其爲勤噫此所以爲念之深也時熊
頵用子文以紓難固仲父耦也撓鄭甞齊與純
門之櫱異矣齊何甞一日忘鄭哉養威蓄謀定
交徵詞萬全而後逞固善用其霸之術而庶幾
王者之事然豈誠有遺力哉德則不競是以功
烈如彼而申侯濤塗之及且紛紛矣然則經之
punctuated: 威。簡書之急，雖不卽及於鄭，然而形禁勢格，使自爲解者，桓其慮之深矣；撻伐之威，雖不卽懲於荊，然而經營圖合，戢而時動者，桓其籌之審矣。折衝於壇坫之上，而仗義以遺諸姬之安，異日孔叔完守，度德而不忍棄者，非以齊有勤我之力與？不然，鄭患方棘，能不遄其南向之轍耶？指顧於俎豆之間，而先聲以摧江漢之焰，異日屈完納款，徼好而惟恐後者，非以齊有制彼之慮與？不然，楚氛方惡，能遽遏其北方之圖耶？故兹會也，在魯人敗邾之師，有愆義干盟之咎；而齊桓謀鄭之念，爲安夏攘夷之勤。是故紀會以美之，而魯之罪比事見矣。抑楚師三至而齊救不至，惡在其爲勤？噫！此所以爲念之深也。時熊頵用子文以紓難，固仲父耦也，撓鄭甞齊，與純門之櫱異矣。齊何甞一日忘鄭哉？養威蓄謀，定交徵詞，萬全而後逞，固善用其霸之術，而庶幾王者之事。然豈誠有遺力哉？德則不競，是以功烈如彼，而申侯、濤塗之及且紛紛矣。然則經之
translation_en:
…might. Although the urgency of his written dispatches did not immediately reach Zheng, yet by constraining the situation and checking the balance of power so as to make the crisis resolve itself, how deep was Duke Huan's foresight! Although the might of punitive expeditions did not immediately chastise Jing [Chu], yet by planning and working toward coalition, holding back and moving only at the right moment, how careful was Duke Huan's calculation! Repelling the enemy from above the diplomatic altar and upholding righteousness to bequeath peace to the various states of the Ji clan—when on a later day Kongshu maintained intact defenses, measuring virtue and not bearing to abandon [Qi], was it not because Qi had exerted itself on their behalf? Otherwise, when Zheng's troubles were so urgent, how could it have avoided hastening its chariot tracks southward [to submit to Chu]? Directing affairs amidst the ceremonial vessels and using his advance reputation to crush the flames along the Jiang and Han rivers—when on a later day Qu Wan offered terms, seeking amity and fearing only to be late, was it not because Qi had the foresight to hold them in check? Otherwise, when Chu's menace was so fierce, how could its designs on the north have been so suddenly halted?

Therefore, in this meeting, on the part of the men of Lu who defeated the army of Zhu, there was the fault of violating righteousness and offending against the covenant; whereas Duke Huan of Qi's concern in planning for Zheng was diligent effort toward pacifying the central states and repelling the barbarians. Thus the Classic records the meeting to praise him, while Lu's offense becomes evident by comparing the events.

Yet the armies of Chu came three times and Qi's relief did not arrive—wherein lay his diligence? Alas! This is precisely why his concern was so deep. At that time Xiong Yun [King Cheng of Chu] employed Ziwen to relieve their difficulties—truly a match for Father Zhong [Guan Zhong]—harassing Zheng to test Qi, which was quite different from the sprout of calamity at the Chun Gate. How could Qi have forgotten Zheng for even a single day? Nurturing his might and storing up plans, solidifying alliances and summoning charges, acting only when completely certain of success—he truly made good use of the arts of a hegemon, and came close to the deeds of a true king. Yet did he really hold back any strength? His virtue was not sufficient to prevail, and therefore his achievements were merely such as they were, while the troubles involving Marquis Shen and [Yuan] Taotu followed one after another in confusion. This being so, when the Classic…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
與桓其取節耶
宋公陳侯衛侯曹伯會晉師于棐林伐鄭
宣公元年公會晉師于瓦定公八年
瞿九思
同考試官教諭左批本傳重衆書法最難發揮是作
詞理明透必究心於經學者
考試官教授黃批能知謹權大旨
考試官教授郭批凜然見抑臣之意
春秋兩紀兵好而均略伯國之臣凡以謹大權
===
也夫用衆非人臣所得專也宜經於棐林于瓦
之役而兩示其義與昔棐林之役晉討鄭也趙
盾將之瓦之會晉救魯也士鞅將之吾聞大夫
與師其體敵今二卿之董是役將非不尊也何
獨言會晉師耶蓋兵權有國之司命君執此以
馭臣臣而敢專之非有國之利也盾之伐鄭也
執言以討貳于時閫外之寄彼其制之然總表
裏之山河而作維辟之威者有晉靈在焉盾雖
位上卿執國命固不得私有其衆也鞅之救魯
punctuated:
與桓，其取節耶？

宋公、陳侯、衛侯、曹伯會晉師于棐林，伐鄭。宣公元年。公會晉師于瓦。定公八年。
瞿九思
同考試官教諭左批：本傳重衆書法最難發揮，是作詞理明透，必究心於經學者。
考試官教授黃批：能知謹權大旨。
考試官教授郭批：凜然見抑臣之意。

《春秋》兩紀兵好，而均略伯國之臣，凡以謹大權也。夫用衆非人臣所得專也，宜經於棐林、于瓦之役，而兩示其義與！昔棐林之役，晉討鄭也，趙盾將之；瓦之會，晉救魯也，士鞅將之。吾聞大夫與師，其體敵；今二卿之董是役，將非不尊也，何獨言「會晉師」耶？蓋兵權，有國之司命，君執此以馭臣；臣而敢專之，非有國之利也。盾之伐鄭也，執言以討貳，于時閫外之寄，彼其制之；然總表裏之山河而作維辟之威者，有晉靈在焉，盾雖位上卿、執國命，固不得私有其衆也。鞅之救魯
translation_en:
… approval of Duke Huan of Qi—was it not a matter of commending a single merit?

"The Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, and the Earl of Cao met the army of Jin at Feilin and attacked Zheng" (first year of Duke Xuan). "The Duke met the army of Jin at Wa" (eighth year of Duke Ding).
Qu Jiusi 瞿九思
Associate Examiner and Instructor Zuo comments: In this commentary, the historiographical principle of emphasizing the multitude is the most difficult to expound. This essay is clear and penetrating in both diction and reasoning; its author must be one who has devoted his mind to the study of the Classics.
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Huang comments: Able to grasp the grand purport of carefully guarding sovereign authority.
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Guo comments: Awe-inspiringly reveals the intention of restraining subjects.

The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) twice records military meetings of amity and in both cases omits the names of the ministers of the hegemonic state; all of this is in order to carefully guard supreme authority. Now, the deployment of the multitude is not something that a subject is permitted to monopolize. How fitting it is that in the campaigns of Feilin and Wa, the Classic twice sets forth this principle! In the past, the campaign at Feilin was Jin's punitive expedition against Zheng, and Zhao Dun 趙盾 commanded it; the meeting at Wa was Jin's relief of Lu, and Shi Yang 士鞅 commanded it. I have heard that in status a Grand Master and an army are equals. Now, when these two ministers directed these campaigns, the commanders were by no means of low rank; why then does the text solely say "met the army of Jin"? This is because military authority is the arbiter of destiny for a state. The ruler holds it in order to control his subjects; if a subject dares to monopolize it, it is not to the advantage of the state. When Dun attacked Zheng, he upheld righteous words to punish a duplicitous state, and at the time, the commission beyond the threshold was under his control. Yet the one who encompassed the mountains and rivers within and without and exercised the majesty that belongs solely to the sovereign was Duke Ling of Jin 晉靈. Although Dun held the rank of Senior Minister and wielded the state's commands, he certainly could not treat the multitude as his private possession. When Yang rescued Lu…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
也仗義以恤患于時師中之命彼其承之然擅
一國之靈寵而作維辟之福者有晉定在焉鞅
雖植根深用物弘又不得上專其權也彼其列
國號召而伯叔與同誠惟知有盾而已今則略
其將而稱師若不知有盾然者蓋忌上侵之偪
為社稷而貴其民耳諸卿同仇而我公于邁誠
惟知有鞅而已今則稱師以蔽將若未嘗會鞅
然者蓋懲君側之横為邦本而重其衆耳再致
嚴於書法非特以繫之於會師將不得並舉之
===
文也又非特別之於君親將不言帥師之例也
直重大衆以抑臣以明人臣不得用衆也此義
明攬權不移在上無贅旒之勢共命不貳在下
無竊柄之姦豈惟戒履霜於晉之卿而厚施盡
征如田季者皆臣道之所不敢出也其為慮遠
矣雖然重衆之義君不得而輕用之況自諸侯
出乎然則兵可弭耶噫顧治本何如耳采薇出
車之意不在天保以前而車攻采芑諸篇寔致
中興之盛不然忘武備者弱國而中制者無功
punctuated: 也，仗義以恤患，于時師中之命，彼其承之；然擅一國之靈寵而作維辟之福者，有晉定在焉，鞅雖植根深、用物弘，又不得上專其權也。彼其列國號召，而伯叔與同，誠惟知有盾而已；今則略其將而稱師，若不知有盾然者，蓋忌上侵之偪，為社稷而貴其民耳。諸卿同仇，而我公于邁，誠惟知有鞅而已；今則稱師以蔽將，若未嘗會鞅然者，蓋懲君側之横，為邦本而重其衆耳。再致嚴於書法，非特以繫之於會，師、將不得並舉之文也；又非特別之於君親將，不言帥師之例也。直重大衆以抑臣，以明人臣不得用衆也。此義明，攬權不移，在上無贅旒之勢；共命不貳，在下無竊柄之姦。豈惟戒履霜於晉之卿，而厚施盡征如田、季者，皆臣道之所不敢出也，其為慮遠矣。雖然，重衆之義，君不得而輕用之，況自諸侯出乎？然則兵可弭耶？噫！顧治本何如耳。《采薇》、《出車》之意，不在《天保》以前；而《車攻》、《采芑》諸篇，寔致中興之盛。不然，忘武備者弱國，而中制者無功。
translation_en: … [As for] his rescuing Lu, he upheld righteousness to relieve distress, and at the time he received the command in the midst of the army; yet the one who possessed the sacred favor of the entire state and dispensed the blessings that belong solely to the sovereign was Duke Ding of Jin (Jin Ding). Even though [Shi] Yang had deep roots and made broad use of resources, he still could not usurp authority from his superior. When he issued the call to the various states and the elder and younger uncles joined together, they truly knew only of the existence of [Zhao] Dun; now, however, [the Spring and Autumn Annals] omits the commander and refers only to the "army," as if it did not know of [Zhao] Dun at all—this was simply because it feared the encroachment of upward usurpation, and for the sake of the altars of soil and grain it valued the people. When the various ministers shared a common enmity and our Duke went forth on the march, they truly knew only of the existence of [Shi] Yang; now, however, it refers to the "army" to obscure the commander, as if they had never met with [Shi] Yang at all—this was simply to chastise the arrogance of those at the ruler's side, and for the sake of the foundation of the state it attached weight to the multitude. Twice exercising such strictness in historiographical phrasing was not merely a matter of the textual rule that when attached to a "meeting" (hui), both "army" and "commander" cannot be mentioned together; nor was it merely to distinguish it from the precedent where, when a ruler personally commands, one does not say "leading an army." Rather, it directly attached weight to the great multitude in order to curb the ministers, thereby making it clear that a subject-minister may not make personal use of the multitude. When this principle is made clear, the grasp of authority does not shift, and above there is no ruler reduced to a mere pendant on a banner; orders are obeyed without duplicity, and below there is no villainy that steals the handle of power. How could this merely be a warning against "treading on frost" [the early signs of usurpation] among the ministers of Jin? Even those who lavished private bounty and monopolized military levies like the Tian clan [of Qi] and the Jisun clan [of Lu] would not dare to embark upon such a course under the Way of the minister—so far-reaching was the Sage's concern! Even so, according to the principle of attaching weight to the multitude, even the ruler himself may not lightly employ them—how much less when military expeditions proceed from the feudal lords! That being so, can arms be abolished altogether? Alas, it depends only on how the fundamental basis of governance is handled! The intent of the odes "Plucking Bracken" (Caiwei) and "Bringing Out the Carts" (Chuche) did not come before "Heaven Protects" (Tianbao); and the pieces "Our Chariots Are Strong" (Chegong) and "Plucking White Millet" (Caiqi) truly brought about the flourishing of the restoration. Otherwise, those who forget military preparedness weaken the state, while those who subject generals to remote control from the court achieve no merit. …

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
後之爲國者毋徒曰重衆云
禮記
內和而外順則民瞻其顏色而弗與爭也
望其容貌而民不生易慢焉故德煇動
於內而民莫不承聽理發諸外而民莫
不承順
鄒觀光
同考試官教諭陳批禮樂和順之應難於形容是作
獨得之可以式矣
===
考試官教授黃批不事雕刻自然成文
考試官教授郭批辭意冲粹必有和順之實者
論君子禮樂之德盛而感乎人者深焉蓋和順
禮樂之德也德盛而感人之深夫乃機之必然
者乎嘗謂禮樂之道體之於己則皇極建推之
於民則王化行顧君子致之何如耳玆惟樂曰
內和則其治心者臻安久天神之妙而太和之
德洽浹於中矣禮曰外順則其治躬者造莊敬
嚴威之實而大順之德昭宣於外矣由是而徵
punctuated:
後之爲國者，毋徒曰「重衆」云。

《禮記》
「內和而外順，則民瞻其顏色而弗與爭也；望其容貌，而民不生易慢焉。故德煇動於內，而民莫不承聽；理發諸外，而民莫不承順。」
鄒觀光
同考試官教諭陳批：禮樂和順之應難於形容，是作獨得之，可以式矣。
考試官教授黃批：不事雕刻，自然成文。
考試官教授郭批：辭意冲粹，必有和順之實者。

論君子禮樂之德盛，而感乎人者深焉。蓋和順，禮樂之德也。德盛而感人之深，夫乃機之必然者乎？嘗謂禮樂之道，體之於己則皇極建，推之於民則王化行，顧君子致之何如耳。玆惟樂曰「內和」，則其治心者，臻安久天神之妙，而太和之德洽浹於中矣；禮曰「外順」，則其治躬者，造莊敬嚴威之實，而大順之德昭宣於外矣。由是而徵
translation_en:
… Those who govern states in later generations must not merely speak of "attaching weight to the multitude."

Record of Rites (Liji)
"When there is harmony within and compliance without, the people gaze upon his countenance and do not contend with him; they look toward his demeanor and the people do not conceive feelings of lightness or disrespect. Therefore, when the radiance of virtue stirs within, there are none among the people who do not attend and listen; when patterned order issues forth without, there are none among the people who do not comply and obey."
Zou Guanguang 鄒觀光
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Chen's comment: The response to the harmony and compliance of rites and music is difficult to describe; this composition alone captures it and may serve as a model.
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Huang's comment: Without resorting to artificial carving, it naturally forms fine writing.
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Guo's comment: The diction and meaning are serene and pure; the author must be one who possesses the substance of harmony and compliance.

This discusses how the gentleman's virtue in rites and music is abundant, and thus his influence upon others is profound. Now, harmony and compliance are the virtues of rites and music. When virtue is abundant and moves others deeply, is this not an inevitable working of things? I have maintained that as for the Way of rites and music, when embodied in oneself, the Supreme Standard is established; when extended to the people, kingly transformation proceeds—it simply depends on how the gentleman brings them to perfection. Here, because music is called "harmony within," his regulation of the mind reaches the wondrousness of tranquil permanence and heavenly spirit, and the virtue of Great Harmony thoroughly permeates the interior; because ritual is called "compliance without," his regulation of the person attains the substance of solemn reverence and stern majesty, and the virtue of Great Compliance is brightly manifested on the exterior. When from this it is verified…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
諸庶民也將見至和見於顏色而瞻之者以和
應和忿戾之氣自融焉孰與爭乎至順見於容
貌而望之者以順應順怠忽之私自弭焉孰生
易慢乎然不但已也君子之德形則著著則明
而斯民之心動則變變則化故至德之輝動之
於內而英華顯文明之盛雖未始期聽於民也
而民莫不承聽焉法君子之和以治心若有機
焉以通之而四海之內同愛矣感人心而太和
豈但不爭已耶至順之理發之於外而儀度昭
===
淑慎之章雖未始期順於民也而民莫不承順
焉法君子之順以治身若有機焉以率之而四
海之內合敬矣定民志而順治豈但不慢已耶
此禮樂之道所以爲大而君子不可斯須去身
也古者聖人象天地而作禮樂因性情而立節
制內外一道也和順一德也感應一機也一者
何吾之心是已故曰無體之禮無聲之樂天子
中和之極聖人位育之功皆是物也否則鐘皷
云樂玉帛云禮其於化民之道遠矣有志於禮
punctuated: 諸庶民也，將見至和見於顏色，而瞻之者以和應和，忿戾之氣自融焉，孰與爭乎？至順見於容貌，而望之者以順應順，怠忽之私自弭焉，孰生易慢乎？然不但已也。君子之德，形則著，著則明；而斯民之心，動則變，變則化。故至德之輝動之於內，而英華顯文明之盛，雖未始期聽於民也，而民莫不承聽焉；法君子之和以治心，若有機焉以通之，而四海之內同愛矣。感人心而太和，豈但不爭已耶？至順之理發之於外，而儀度昭淑慎之章，雖未始期順於民也，而民莫不承順焉；法君子之順以治身，若有機焉以率之，而四海之內合敬矣。定民志而順治，豈但不慢已耶？此禮樂之道所以爲大，而君子不可斯須去身也。古者聖人象天地而作禮樂，因性情而立節制，內外一道也，和順一德也，感應一機也。一者何？吾之心是已。故曰：「無體之禮，無聲之樂。」天子中和之極，聖人位育之功，皆是物也。否則，鐘皷云樂，玉帛云禮，其於化民之道遠矣。有志於禮…
translation_en: …in the common people, one will see supreme harmony appear in his countenance, so that those who look upon him respond to harmony with harmony; angry and perverse qi naturally melts away—who then would contend with him? Supreme compliance will appear in his demeanor, so that those who gaze upon him respond to compliance with compliance; lazy and neglectful selfishness naturally ceases—who then would give rise to contempt or disrespect? Yet it does not stop even here. As for the virtue of the noble man, once given form it becomes manifest, and once manifest it becomes luminous; as for the minds of these people, once moved they change, and once changed they are transformed. Therefore, when the radiance of supreme virtue stirs within, and its finest blossoms display the flourishing of civil culture, although he never initially expects the people to heed him, none of the people fail to heed and follow him. Emulating the noble man's harmony in governing their own minds, it is as if there were a subtle mechanism connecting them, and within the four seas all share in mutual affection. Moving human hearts to reach great harmony—how could this merely be a matter of not contending? When the principle of supreme compliance issues forth on the outside, and his deportment displays the emblems of gentle caution, although he never initially expects the people to comply with him, none of the people fail to comply and submit. Emulating the noble man's compliance in governing their own persons, it is as if there were a subtle mechanism leading them, and within the four seas all unite in reverence. Settling the people's will and achieving compliant order—how could this merely be a matter of not being disrespectful? This is why the Way of rites and music is great, and why the noble man may not let them leave his person even for an instant. In antiquity, the sages modeled themselves on Heaven and Earth to create rites and music, and followed human nature and feelings to establish regulations and restraints: inner and outer are a single Way, harmony and compliance are a single virtue, and stimulus and response are a single mechanism. What is this oneness? It is simply our own mind. Thus it is said: "Rites without physical form, music without sound." The Son of Heaven's perfection of centrality and harmony, and the sage's achievement of establishing the cosmic order and nurturing all things, are all this very thing. Otherwise, if bells and drums are what is called music, and jade and silk are what is called rites, how far removed that is from the Way of transforming the people! Those who set their minds on rites…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
樂者審所尚哉
王言如絲其出如綸
王同晉
同考試官教諭陳批絲綸字當有斟酌此作最善形
容可錄
考試官教授黃批得慎王言意
考試官教授郭批簡而文
王者之言微而著其當慎可知矣甚矣王言之
所係匪輕也如綸由於如絲則微者著矣是可
===
以弗慎乎哉記緇衣者以爲人君身居天位則
必口代天言吾嘗擬而議之而知王言之當慎
矣蓋其鼓舞天下不容恭默而無言也故嘗闡
心思之秘而秩之德音敷化理之原而宣之巽
命聲必爲律其旨精矣而方發於宮庭猶近於
微而未顯言必中倫其義密矣而方形於朝宁
猶涉於隱而未章象其小焉不過如絲而已矣
然王者之尊天下之所聽命故其言一出而其
機自通王者之令天下之所祗承故其發雖邇
punctuated:
樂者，審所尚哉。

王言如絲，其出如綸。
王同晉
同考試官教諭陳批：絲綸字當有斟酌，此作最善形容，可錄。
考試官教授黃批：得慎王言意。
考試官教授郭批：簡而文。

王者之言，微而著，其當慎可知矣。甚矣！王言之所係匪輕也。如綸由於如絲，則微者著矣，是可以弗慎乎哉？記《緇衣》者以爲：人君身居天位，則必口代天言。吾嘗擬而議之，而知王言之當慎矣。蓋其鼓舞天下，不容恭默而無言也。故嘗闡心思之秘，而秩之德音；敷化理之原，而宣之巽命。聲必爲律，其旨精矣，而方發於宮庭，猶近於微而未顯；言必中倫，其義密矣，而方形於朝宁，猶涉於隱而未章。象其小焉，不過如絲而已矣。然王者之尊，天下之所聽命，故其言一出，而其機自通；王者之令，天下之所祗承，故其發雖邇，
translation_en:
… [those who aspire to rites and] music should carefully examine what they esteem!

"The king's words are like silk threads; when they go forth, they are like cords."
Wang Tongjin
Associate Examiner and Instructor Chen commented: "The words 'silk threads' and 'cords' call for careful weighing. This composition describes them best and is worthy of selection."
Examiner and Confucian School Director Huang commented: "Captures the meaning of being cautious with the king's words."
Examiner and Confucian School Director Guo commented: "Concise and refined."

The words of a true king are subtle yet become manifest; that he must be cautious with them can thus be known. Profound indeed! What depends upon the king's words is no light matter. That their being like cords arises from their being like silk threads means that what is subtle becomes manifest—how then could one not be cautious?

The recorder of the "Black Robes" ("Ziyi" chapter of the Book of Rites) held that since the ruler of men occupies the heavenly position in person, his mouth must speak on behalf of Heaven. I have considered and discussed this, and thereby know that the king's words must be treated with caution. For in inspiring and rousing all under Heaven, he cannot merely remain in reverent silence without speaking. Therefore, he unfolds the secrets of his heart's thoughts and orders them as virtuous pronouncements; he spreads forth the principles of transformative governance and proclaims them as compliant commands. His voice must serve as a standard pitch—its purport is refined indeed; yet when first uttered within the palace court, it is still close to being subtle and not yet manifest. His words must accord with moral principles—their meaning is dense indeed; yet when first taking form in the court audience hall, they still border on the hidden and are not yet illustrious. Likening them to something small, they are no more than silk threads. Yet the dignity of the true king is that from which all under Heaven await commands; thus, once his words go forth, their vital mechanism naturally communicates itself everywhere. The orders of the true king are what all under Heaven reverently receive; thus, although their issuance is near at hand…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
而其傳自遠經綸之蘊以言而宣雖未極于敷
錫之大也仰君德之章聞而誦聖謨者罔或後
焉微而斯顯有若吐之方為絲而播之即為綸
矣彌綸之功以言而達雖未極于訓行之廣也
仰治典之敷布而遵帝訓者罔或違焉隱而斯
章有若始于絲之小而繼以綸之大矣要之王
人有絲綸之命斯天下有經緯之文言固不可
已也惟其出之如綸則當於如絲之初而慎之
爾况其言有不止於絲焉則其出又當何如者
===
而烏可以游言倡哉雖然未已也由是左史紀
焉後世述焉孰非是言哉故伊尹告商王曰大
哉王言而又曰一哉王心何者心固所以出言
者也欲慎言者立誠以脩辭則言寡尤而天下
法矣
第貳場
論
君志定而天下之治成
李登
punctuated:
而其傳自遠。經綸之蘊，以言而宣，雖未極于敷錫之大也，仰君德之章聞，而誦聖謨者罔或後焉。微而斯顯，有若吐之方為絲，而播之即為綸矣。彌綸之功，以言而達，雖未極于訓行之廣也，仰治典之敷布，而遵帝訓者罔或違焉。隱而斯章，有若始于絲之小，而繼以綸之大矣。要之，王人有絲綸之命，斯天下有經緯之文，言固不可已也。惟其出之如綸，則當於如絲之初而慎之爾。况其言有不止於絲焉，則其出又當何如者，而烏可以游言倡哉？雖然，未已也。由是左史紀焉，後世述焉，孰非是言哉？故伊尹告商王曰：「大哉王言！」而又曰：「一哉王心！」何者？心固所以出言者也。欲慎言者，立誠以脩辭，則言寡尤而天下法矣。

第貳場
論
君志定而天下之治成
李登
translation_en:
…yet their transmission naturally reaches afar. The deep substance of ordering governance is proclaimed through words; although it has not yet reached the utmost greatness of universal bestowal, those who look up to the manifest renown of the ruler’s virtue and recite his sage counsels will never lag behind. From the subtle it thus becomes manifest, just as what is spun out at first as fine silk threads becomes, once spread abroad, a braided cord.
