That Yizhou should be distantly assigned to Wei, and Jizhou assigned to tiny Wey; that Yan in the north is paired with the Ximu [Split Wood] Jupiter station in the east, and Lu in the east is paired with the Jianglou [Descending Bond] station in the west; that Qin in the northwest has its Chunshou [Quail's Head] station lodged in the southeast, while Wu and Yue in the southeast have their Xingji [Stellar Era] station lodged in the northeast—even since antiquity people have doubted these correspondences. How much more so today, when the two provinces of Jingzhou and Yangzhou make up half the territory of the realm, and their households, population, and notable figures actually account for eight-tenths of the empire—how could the celestial degrees fail to shift downward accordingly? Moreover, during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, each state corresponded astrologically to its own territory; now that feudal commanderies and kingdoms have been abolished and one wishes to match everything entirely to the affairs of the central court, how can every single portent be verified? This is another explanation.

All of these are matters about which Your Reverence harbors doubts. In my humble view, however, Heaven and Earth are vast indeed! Within them, man takes what resembles his own physical form and vital breath and seeks to match them to the cosmos; next he takes the subtle mechanisms that communicate with his own mind and tries to fathom them; and then he takes the mathematical methods by which he can calculate and casts them into models, assuming that all of Heaven and Earth is contained therein. That some things correspond is naturally constant, and that some things fail to correspond is likewise constant. During the Jiajing era (1522–1566), comets and portents like the Banner of Chiyou trespassed everywhere in the heavens; between Shanxi and Shaanxi …

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
間坼地千里摧百萬人之命夏霜冬雹水
旱霆火靡歲無之遠方波臣不得盡覩脩
省之實而宗伯所陳事非瑞芝即白龜鹿
也私心固不勝其憂矣而十載之內歲益
登綱紀益振朝野益恬穆無事豈所謂不
在天而在人者蓋有道耶抑
高皇帝之功德貽後者與宇宙並而災祥不能
撼耶客歲象異特小小耳既非五星之精
所化不過周伯王蓬之屬而其在閣道上
===
下者占不過夷狄寇竊伏姦在側耳
聖主喆輔公卿臺諫恐然而交相戒者何也愚
有以窺其故矣夫人主之攝下也無所不
靡而其於言動也無所不快意蓋天下讓
尊焉使非有更尊而為天者以臨之而又
出災異以警示之幾何而不日流於驕且
怠耶不然徹樂避殿減膳菲服要亦責躬
之虛文而所謂求言宥過賜租省刑亦有
國之常政又何必待示變而始克舉也是
punctuated: 間，坼地千里，摧百萬人之命；夏霜冬雹，水旱霆火，靡歲無之。遠方波臣，不得盡覩脩省之實，而宗伯所陳事，非瑞芝即白龜鹿也，私心固不勝其憂矣。而十載之內，歲益登，綱紀益振，朝野益恬穆無事。豈所謂不在天而在人者，蓋有道耶？抑高皇帝之功德貽後者，與宇宙並，而災祥不能撼耶？客歲象異，特小小耳，既非五星之精所化，不過周伯、王蓬之屬；而其在閣道上下者，占不過夷狄寇竊、伏姦在側耳。聖主、喆輔、公卿、臺諫恐然而交相戒者，何也？愚有以窺其故矣。夫人主之攝下也，無所不靡；而其於言動也，無所不快意，蓋天下讓尊焉。使非有更尊而為天者以臨之，而又出災異以警示之，幾何而不日流於驕且怠耶？不然，徹樂、避殿、減膳、菲服，要亦責躬之虛文；而所謂求言、宥過、賜租、省刑，亦有國之常政，又何必待示變而始克舉也？是
translation_en: …region [of Shanxi and Shaanxi], the earth split open for a thousand li, destroying the lives of a million people; summer frosts and winter hail, floods, droughts, thunderbolts, and fires—not a year went by without them. As a humble subject in a distant region, I could not fully witness the reality of court self-cultivation and introspection, while the matters presented by the Minister of Rites were nothing if not auspicious fungi or white tortoises and deer; in my private heart I could not overcome my worry. Yet within ten years, the harvests have grown ever more abundant, the laws and discipline ever more invigorated, and court and countryside ever more tranquil and free of trouble. Could it be that what is called "resting not with Heaven, but with man" indeed has a Way to it? Or is it that the merits and virtue bequeathed to posterity by the Exalted Emperor (Gao huangdi, i.e., Emperor Taizu) are coequal with the cosmos, so that calamities and portents cannot shake them? The celestial anomalies of last year were merely minor ones. Since they were not transformed from the essences of the Five Planets, they were nothing more than stars of the sort of Zhoubo or Wangpeng; and as for their appearing above and below the Gedao constellation, the prognostication is nothing more than raids and thefts by barbarian tribes or hidden traitors at the ruler's side. Why is it, then, that our sage ruler, wise grand counselors, ministers, and Censorate and Remonstrance officials are all fearful and mutually admonish one another? Humble as I am, I have been able to discern the reason. When a ruler of men holds sway over his subordinates, there is nothing that does not bend before him; and in his words and actions, there is nothing that does not gratify his wishes, for the whole world yields supremacy to him. Were it not that there is One even more supreme—namely Heaven—overlooking him above, and furthermore sending forth calamities and anomalies to warn and admonish him, how long would it take before he daily slid into arrogance and indolence? Otherwise, removing music, vacating the main hall, reducing the imperial table, and wearing coarse garments are in the end mere empty formalities of self-reproach; and what are called seeking直言 [outspoken advice], pardoning faults, remitting taxes, and lightening punishments are also the regular governance of a state—why must one wait until Heaven displays an anomaly before being able to carry them out? Therefore…

title: 萬曆元年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
故人主而能祗敬則大戊之桑榖高宗之
雊雉爲大戊高宗昭德也宋景之熒惑爲
宋景昭言也人主而汰則舎譽彗矣平慮
鬼目矣甘露雀餳矣愚故曰執事之旨不
在天而在人也
第三問
李際春
同考試官學正趙批評論今古如視諸掌且思上資
清瞻裨益治道此豈獨留意史學是有忠愛之忱者録之
===
同考試官敎授周批讀史者非徒資辨洽貴得其精
脩史者非徒循故事要以示信此作獨能折衷是可錄也
考試官敎授黃批有良史之才
考試官敎授郭批有學識而才能發之
愚嘗讀文中子之書曰史之失自遷固始
也記繁而志寡則又未嘗不歎其言之失
也夫經有不必記而史有不必志孔子之
作春秋也而君臣父子夫婦長幼之倫著
焉中國夷狄君子小人之界判焉蓋二百
punctuated:
故人主而能祗敬，則大戊之桑榖、高宗之雊雉，爲大戊、高宗昭德也；宋景之熒惑，爲宋景昭言也。人主而汰，則舎譽彗矣，平慮鬼目矣，甘露雀餳矣。愚故曰：執事之旨不在天而在人也。

第三問
李際春
〔同考試官學正趙批：評論今古，如視諸掌，且思上資清瞻，裨益治道。此豈獨留意史學，是有忠愛之忱者，録之。〕
〔同考試官敎授周批：讀史者非徒資辨洽，貴得其精；脩史者非徒循故事，要以示信。此作獨能折衷，是可錄也。〕
〔考試官敎授黃批：有良史之才。〕
〔考試官敎授郭批：有學識而才能發之。〕

愚嘗讀《文中子》之書曰：「史之失，自遷、固始也，記繁而志寡。」則又未嘗不歎其言之失也。夫經有不必記，而史有不必志。孔子之作《春秋》也，而君臣、父子、夫婦、長幼之倫著焉，中國、夷狄、君子、小人之界判焉，蓋二百
translation_en:
… Therefore, if a ruler is capable of reverent awe, then the mulberry and grain trees that grew together under Taiwu and the crowing pheasant under Gaozong served to manifest the virtue of Taiwu and Gaozong; and Mars lingering in the Heart mansion under Duke Jing of Song served to manifest the worthy words of Duke Jing of Song. If a ruler is extravagant and arrogant, then the auspicious Sheyu star is no better than a comet, the auspicious pinglü tree no better than a weed [guimu], and sweet dew no better than sparrow-malt [quexing]. For this reason I say that the intent of Your Honor's question lies not in Heaven, but in man.

The Third Policy Question
Li Jichun 
[Comment by Associate Examiner Department Director of Schools Zhao: He evaluates past and present as clearly as looking at the palm of his hand, and moreover seeks to provide material for the Emperor's pure gaze and benefit the way of governance. How is this merely paying attention to historiography? He possesses genuine loyalty and devotion; record it.]
[Comment by Associate Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Zhou: One who reads history does not merely use it for broad disputation, but values grasping its essence; one who compiles history does not merely follow precedent, but aims to establish trustworthiness. This essay alone manages to strike a judicious balance, and is worthy of being recorded.]
[Comment by Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Huang: He possesses the talent of a fine historian.]
[Comment by Examiner Prefectural Director of Schools Guo: He has learning and insight, and his talent is able to bring them forth.]

I once read in the book of Master Wenzhong (Wenzhongzi): "The failings of history began with Sima Qian and Ban Gu: their records of events are profuse, while their expression of moral principles is scant." Yet I have never failed to sigh over the error of this remark. Now, the Classics have things they do not need to record, and histories have principles they do not need to spell out. When Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), the moral relationships between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, and elder and younger were made manifest therein, and the boundaries between the Central States and the barbarians, the gentleman and the petty man, were distinguished therein.
